# API Automation Testing with Vitest
## A Practical Guide to Testing Modern REST APIs with TypeScript

*From your first assertion to a production-ready test suite*

---

## Preface

There is a specific kind of frustration that every developer encounters at some point in their career. You have built something that works. You tested it manually — you opened the browser, filled in the form, watched the response come back. Everything looked fine. You deployed it. Three days later, a user reports that the sign-in endpoint returns a 500 error when the username contains an apostrophe. Or a colleague refactors the authentication middleware and breaks the session token format. Or a third-party service changes its response shape and your API silently starts returning null for a field that ten other services depend on.

You did not catch it because you cannot manually test everything, every time, before every deployment. No human can. And yet the consequences of not catching these things are real: data corruption, security vulnerabilities shipping to production, broken integrations that users discover before you do.

This book exists because there is a gap — a specific, teachable, closeable gap — between knowing how to write code and knowing how to verify that code behaves correctly over HTTP. That gap is API automation testing.

API automation testing is not a niche skill. It is not something reserved for dedicated QA engineers at large companies. It is something every developer who touches a REST API should know how to do, because it is the single most effective way to protect the behavior of a system over time. Not unit tests, which test isolated functions in artificial isolation. Not end-to-end browser tests, which are slow, brittle, and expensive to maintain. API tests occupy the sweet spot: they test real deployed code, through the real HTTP interface, in a way that is fast, reliable, and directly tied to what users actually experience.

This book will teach you that skill from the ground up.

You do not need prior testing experience. You do not need to be a TypeScript expert. You need basic JavaScript familiarity and a willingness to think carefully about what it means for software to be correct. By the time you finish this book, you will be able to design a test suite for any REST API, write tests that are readable and maintainable, catch regressions before they reach production, and reason clearly about what your tests do and do not prove.

The API we test throughout this book is a real, deployed chat application called Chatty, running at `https://api.codeandtest.com/api/v1`. It has authentication, user profiles, posts, reactions, followers, images — a realistic surface area that exposes the full range of challenges you will encounter in production API testing. Every code example in this book runs against that live API. Every exercise produces real output. There is no toy server, no mock data, no pretend environment. You are testing a real system from page one.

We use Vitest as our test runner, Axios as our HTTP client, and TypeScript for type safety. These are not arbitrary choices — each one is explained and justified. We use them because they make tests easier to write, easier to read, and easier to maintain. That is the only criterion that matters.

A note on philosophy: this book teaches testing as a thinking skill, not just a coding skill. Knowing the Vitest API is table stakes. The harder and more valuable skill is knowing *what* to test, *how much* to test, *when* to test, and *why* a given assertion actually protects you against real failures. We will spend as much time on those questions as on the mechanics of writing test code.

---

## How to Read This Book

This book is divided into four parts.

**Part I: Foundations** covers everything you need to understand before writing a single test. What API testing is and why it matters. How HTTP works at the level of detail that testing requires. What tools we use and why.

**Part II: Writing Your First Tests** takes you from zero to working tests against a real API. The anatomy of a test. How to make assertions. How to handle authentication. How to structure a test file.

**Part III: Real-World Patterns** covers the scenarios you encounter constantly in practice: testing authenticated endpoints, test data lifecycle management, testing CRUD operations, testing error conditions, and testing security properties.

**Part IV: Production-Ready Test Suites** covers the engineering work that turns a collection of test files into a professional test suite: configuration, CI/CD integration, reporting, coverage, and long-term maintenance.

**Chapter dependencies** are linear within each part. Chapter 5 assumes Chapter 4. You can skip ahead if you have prior experience, but the foundational chapters are shorter than you might expect and contain assumptions that later chapters build on.

**Prerequisites**: You should be comfortable reading and writing JavaScript, including async/await syntax. You should understand what a function is, what an object is, and what an array is. That is genuinely all you need.

**What you do not need**: Prior testing experience of any kind. TypeScript experience — we introduce TypeScript features as they appear and explain each one. Prior experience with any specific API testing tool. A locally running server — we test against `https://api.codeandtest.com/api/v1` throughout.

**A practical note on exercises**: Every chapter ends with exercises. Do them. Reading about testing is useful. Writing tests is transformative. The exercises are designed to take 15–45 minutes each and produce working code. The solution for every exercise exists in the course repository.

# Part I: Foundations

---

## Chapter 1: What Is API Testing and Why It Matters

Before you can write effective tests, you need a clear model of what you are testing and why. This chapter builds that model.

### 1.1 The Testing Pyramid

The testing pyramid is a mental model for thinking about different kinds of automated tests. It was first described by Mike Cohn in 2009 and remains one of the most useful frameworks for thinking about test strategy.

The pyramid has three layers.

At the base — the widest layer — are **unit tests**. Unit tests test individual functions or classes in isolation, with all external dependencies replaced by test doubles (mocks, stubs, fakes). A unit test for a function that validates an email address calls that function with various inputs and checks the return values. No database. No network. No file system. Unit tests are fast (thousands per second), cheap to write, and deterministic. They are the appropriate tool for verifying algorithmic correctness: parsing logic, calculation logic, validation logic, transformation logic. A well-tested codebase typically has hundreds or thousands of unit tests.

In the middle is the **integration test** layer. Integration tests test multiple components working together, usually including a real database or a real service but stopping short of full end-to-end flows through a UI. API tests belong in this layer. They are slower than unit tests (network round trips take time) and require a running server, but they test something unit tests cannot: the behavior of the entire system as seen from the outside, through the real HTTP interface.

At the top — the narrowest layer — are **end-to-end (E2E) tests**. E2E tests drive a real browser through real user flows: open the page, type in the form, click the button, wait for the response. Playwright and Cypress are the dominant tools here. E2E tests are the most realistic kind of test — they test exactly what users experience — but they are also the most expensive: slow to run, brittle (UI changes break them), hard to maintain, and difficult to parallelize.

The pyramid metaphor captures a key insight: **you should have more tests at the bottom and fewer at the top**. A healthy test suite might have 500 unit tests, 100 API tests, and 20 E2E tests. The ratio reflects cost and feedback speed, not importance.

API tests occupy the sweet spot. They are realistic — they test real deployed code over a real network. They are also fast enough to run in CI on every pull request. And crucially, they test things that unit tests cannot: HTTP behavior (status codes, headers, cookies), authentication and authorization (does the middleware actually reject unauthenticated requests?), database persistence (does a POST followed by a GET return the right data?), and cross-cutting concerns like rate limiting and CORS.

### 1.2 What Makes an API Test Different

A unit test asks: "Does this function, given this input, return this output?"

An API test asks: "Does this HTTP endpoint, given this request, return the correct response — and leave the system in the correct state?"

The shift matters more than it first appears.

First, you are testing over the network. This means tests are inherently slower and can fail for reasons outside your control: network timeouts, rate limiting, server unavailability. Good API tests are designed to be resilient to transient failures and to fail clearly when they do fail.

Second, you are testing **real deployed code**. Unit tests test isolated functions, which means they can pass even when the system is deeply broken — a mocked database always returns what you tell it to. API tests cannot be fooled this way. If the server is broken, the tests fail. This is precisely the point.

Third, you are testing **what users actually experience**. Users do not call functions. They make HTTP requests and receive HTTP responses. An API test that sends POST `/signin` with a valid username and password and checks that the response contains a valid session cookie is testing exactly what a user's browser does. The test is a specification written in code.

Fourth, testing over HTTP means you must think carefully about **state**. HTTP is stateless — each request is independent. But the system you are testing is not stateless — it has a database, and actions have persistent consequences. Testing a DELETE endpoint means you must first create the resource. Testing a PATCH endpoint means you need to know the current state before and after. Managing this state — creating it for tests, cleaning it up after — is one of the central skills of API testing, and we will spend a full chapter on it.

### 1.3 What You Can Assert

A response from an HTTP API carries a rich payload of information. Most beginners check only the status code. Professional test suites check everything that matters.

**Status codes** are the first thing to check and the most obvious. A POST that creates a resource should return 201, not 200. A request with invalid credentials should return 401, not 500. Status code assertions catch the broadest class of errors: routing failures, missing middleware, authentication bugs, and server crashes.

**Response body — exact values** are appropriate when the value is known and stable. The user's email address does not change between requests. A specific post's author ID is deterministic. The count of a newly created user's posts is exactly zero. These exact assertions are your strongest protection against subtle data corruption.

**Response body — shape and types** are appropriate when exact values are not predictable. A newly registered user's `_id` will be a MongoDB ObjectId string, but you cannot know it in advance. You can still assert that it is a string of the right format. A list of posts may have any length, but you can assert that each item has the expected fields with the expected types.

**Response body — computed relationships** test invariants: the relationship between values. If a user has 3 posts, the postsCount field should be 3. If you follow 5 users, your followingCount should be 5. These assertions catch inconsistencies between stored fields and computed aggregates.

**Response headers** carry important information about authentication (set-cookie), content type (content-type: application/json), caching behavior, and CORS permissions. Testing that set-cookie is present and contains the right flags (HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite) is a security assertion that protects your users.

**Response timing** catches performance regressions. An endpoint that normally responds in 200ms but now takes 5 seconds has a bug — probably a missing database index or an N+1 query. Asserting that responses arrive within a reasonable timeout is a first line of defense.

**Security — what should NOT be there** is one of the most important and most overlooked assertion category. Password hashes must never appear in API responses. Internal IDs, system fields, and sensitive configuration must not leak. These assertions protect your users and your system. `.not.toHaveProperty('password')` is a test worth writing on every endpoint that returns user data.

**State changes** test persistence. After a POST, a subsequent GET should return the created resource. After a DELETE, the resource should be gone. After a PATCH, the changed fields should reflect the update. These round-trip assertions test the full stack: your controller, your service layer, your database queries, and your serialization logic — all in a single test sequence.

### 1.4 The Cost of Not Testing APIs

It is tempting to think of testing as a cost — time spent writing tests is time not spent building features. This framing has the math backwards. The real question is: compared to what?

Compared to manual testing, automated tests are dramatically cheaper over time. A manual test of the sign-in flow takes two minutes. An automated test takes 300 milliseconds. If you test sign-in before every deployment, and you deploy once a day, a manual test costs over 12 hours per year. The automated test costs about 90 seconds of execution time, amortized over the one or two hours it took to write.

But the more important comparison is against the cost of *not* testing.

**Silent data corruption** is the most dangerous failure mode. An API that accepts a malformed PATCH request and silently writes garbage to the database does not immediately produce visible errors. Users notice days or weeks later when queries start returning wrong data. By then, the corruption may have propagated through your system and backups. A test that asserts the exact shape of data written by a PATCH endpoint catches this the moment it is introduced.

**Security vulnerabilities** that ship to production are often simple: a missing authorization check that lets one user access another user's data; a response serializer that accidentally includes a password hash; a rate-limiting bypass that enables brute-force attacks on sign-in. Each of these is trivially testable. None of them survive a test suite that includes security assertions.

**Regressions from refactoring** are the most common day-to-day cost of insufficient testing. A developer renames a database field and updates the model, but forgets to update two of the eight controllers that read it. Unit tests pass — they mock the database. API tests fail — they test the real response. Without those API tests, the regression reaches production.

**Broken integrations discovered in production** are the most expensive kind of failure. Your API is consumed by mobile apps, third-party services, and internal tools. When your API changes a response shape — even a non-breaking addition — downstream consumers can break in unexpected ways. Tests that assert the exact response shape serve as a contract: they break when you accidentally violate the contract you have implicitly made with your consumers.

The cost of writing API tests is real but bounded. The cost of not writing them is unbounded and tends to be paid at the worst possible time.

### 1.5 A Brief History of API Testing Tools

API testing has been possible as long as HTTP has existed. The first tool most developers reach for is **curl** — a command-line tool for making HTTP requests that has been available since 1997. Curl is still useful for quick manual checks, and we will occasionally use it in exercises. But curl output is hard to automate and impossible to maintain at scale.

**Postman** emerged around 2012 as a GUI tool for exploring and testing APIs. Its collection and environment system made it possible to organize and run sequences of requests with assertions. Postman became enormously popular, particularly among QA engineers and developers who were not comfortable writing test code. It remains useful for exploration and documentation. Postman's limitations are real but not fatal: collections are stored as JSON blobs that are hard to review in code review, assertions are written in a custom JavaScript dialect, and the GUI workflow does not compose well with CI/CD pipelines.

**Code-based testing frameworks** — Jest, Mocha, Vitest, Jasmine — combined with HTTP clients — Axios, node-fetch, SuperTest — represent the current state of the art for professional API testing. Writing tests as code means they live in the same repository as the code they test, go through the same code review, benefit from the same version control, and run in the same CI/CD pipeline. Tests written in TypeScript have type safety. Tests that import your domain types can assert against them directly. The full power of the JavaScript ecosystem — faker for test data generation, lodash for data manipulation, custom matchers for domain-specific assertions — is available without plugin systems or workarounds.

**When to use Postman versus code-based tests**: Postman excels at exploration. When you are first encountering an unfamiliar API, Postman's GUI makes it easy to construct requests, inspect responses, and understand the system. Use it for discovery. Write the actual test suite in code. If you are on a team where non-developers need to read and write tests, Postman's accessibility is a real advantage. For everything else — automation, CI/CD integration, long-term maintenance — code-based tests win.

**Key Points**

- The testing pyramid has three layers: unit tests (fast, isolated), integration/API tests (realistic, medium speed), and E2E tests (most realistic, slowest and most brittle).
- API tests test real deployed code through the real HTTP interface, making them highly realistic and effective at catching the bugs that matter most to users.
- You can assert status codes, response body values, response shape, response headers, response timing, security properties (what should not be there), and state changes.
- The cost of not testing APIs is paid in silent data corruption, security vulnerabilities, regressions from refactoring, and broken integrations discovered in production.
- Code-based test frameworks (Vitest + Axios + TypeScript) are superior to GUI tools for long-term maintenance, CI/CD integration, and large-scale test suites.

**Exercises**

1. Think of a web application you have used recently. List five API behaviors that you would want to test if you were responsible for it. For each, write one sentence describing what a failure would look like in production.

2. The statement "unit tests catch more bugs than API tests" is sometimes made by developers who prefer unit testing. Under what circumstances is this true? Under what circumstances is it false? Write a paragraph defending each position.

3. Consider a PATCH /users/:id endpoint that updates a user's display name. List every assertion dimension from Section 1.3 and write one concrete assertion (in plain English) for each dimension against this endpoint.

4. A developer argues that Postman collections checked into git are just as maintainable as Vitest test files checked into git. What are the strongest arguments for and against this position? Which do you find more convincing?

5. Sketch a testing pyramid for a chat application with sign-in, posting, following, and search features. How many tests of each type would you target? What would each E2E test cover that API tests could not?

## Chapter 2: HTTP and REST — The Language of APIs

You cannot test what you do not understand. Before writing a single test, you need a working mental model of how HTTP requests and responses work — at a level of detail that testing requires. This chapter builds that model.

### 2.1 The Request-Response Cycle

When your test calls `axios.post('https://api.codeandtest.com/api/v1/auth/signin', { username: 'alice', password: 'secret' })`, a remarkable sequence of events unfolds.

**DNS resolution**: The HTTP client asks a DNS resolver to convert `api.codeandtest.com` into an IP address. This typically takes a few milliseconds and is cached, so subsequent requests to the same host skip it. The result is something like `76.76.21.164`.

**TCP connection**: The client opens a TCP connection to port 443 (HTTPS) at that IP address. This is a three-way handshake: SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK. It takes one round-trip time (RTT) — perhaps 50ms for a request to a US server from Europe.

**TLS handshake**: Because this is HTTPS, the client and server negotiate an encrypted connection. They exchange certificates, agree on encryption parameters, and derive a shared secret. This takes another 1–2 RTTs. Modern TLS 1.3 completes the handshake in one RTT.

**HTTP request sent**: The client sends the HTTP request over the encrypted connection. The request includes the method, path, headers, and body.

**Server processing**: The server receives the request. Its routing layer directs it to the correct handler. The handler validates the input, queries the database, constructs a response object, and serializes it to JSON. If any of these steps fails, the server constructs an error response instead.

**HTTP response received**: The server sends the HTTP response back over the same connection. The client receives it and your Axios call resolves.

**Connection reuse**: Modern HTTP uses persistent connections (HTTP/1.1 keep-alive or HTTP/2 multiplexing). The TCP connection is not closed after each request; it is kept open for reuse. This is why a sequence of requests to the same host is faster than the first request.

Why does this matter for testing? Several reasons. The 50–200ms round-trip time means API tests are meaningfully slower than unit tests — you must set realistic timeouts. Rate limits are enforced by the server and apply to your test requests just as they apply to production requests, which affects how you structure tests. Connection errors (ECONNREFUSED, ETIMEDOUT) produce a specific class of test failures distinct from HTTP error responses. Understanding these layers helps you diagnose test failures quickly.

### 2.2 Anatomy of an HTTP Request

An HTTP request is a text document with a precise structure. Here is what the raw HTTP request looks like when your test calls `POST /auth/signin`:

```
POST /api/v1/auth/signin HTTP/1.1
Host: api.codeandtest.com
Content-Type: application/json
Accept: application/json, text/plain, */*
Accept-Encoding: gzip, deflate, br
Content-Length: 49
User-Agent: axios/1.6.2
Connection: keep-alive

{"username":"vitest_alice_001","password":"Secret1@3"}
```

The first line is the **request line**: method, path, and HTTP version. The method tells the server what kind of operation this is. The path identifies the resource. HTTP version is almost always HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2.

The lines that follow, before the blank line, are **request headers**. Each header is a key-value pair separated by a colon. The most important headers for API testing:

- `Host`: Required in HTTP/1.1. Tells the server which virtual host is being addressed.
- `Content-Type`: Tells the server how to interpret the request body. For JSON APIs, this should always be `application/json`.
- `Authorization`: Carries authentication credentials. We will see two formats: `Bearer <token>` for JWT-based auth and session-based auth using cookies.
- `Cookie`: Carries cookies, including session cookies. When you authenticate to Chatty and receive a session cookie, subsequent requests carry it here automatically when using Axios with `withCredentials: true`.
- Custom headers like `x-test-secret` used by Chatty's cleanup endpoint to authenticate test infrastructure.

The blank line after the last header separates the headers from the **request body**. Not all requests have a body — GET and DELETE typically do not. POST and PATCH almost always do. When the Content-Type is `application/json`, the body is a JSON-encoded string.

Axios constructs this request from your code automatically. When you write:
```typescript
axios.post(url, { username: 'alice', password: 'secret' }, {
  headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' }
})
```
Axios sets Content-Type, serializes the body to JSON, and sets Content-Length. You never deal with raw HTTP text.

### 2.3 Anatomy of an HTTP Response

Here is the raw HTTP response from a successful `POST /auth/signin`:

```
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8
Set-Cookie: session=eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9...; Path=/; Expires=Sat, 01 Jan 2028 00:00:00 GMT; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax
Content-Length: 312
ETag: "138-8kQvT2ixGz0sV1nLqPO8i7w3Y4I"
Date: Fri, 18 Apr 2026 12:00:00 GMT
Connection: keep-alive

{"message":"User login successfully","user":{"_id":"6612a...","username":"vitest_alice_001","email":"alice@example.com","postsCount":0,"followersCount":0,"followingCount":0}}
```

The first line is the **status line**: HTTP version, status code, and reason phrase. The status code is the most important single piece of information in the response. Your tests should always check it first.

The **response headers** carry metadata. For API testing, the most important:
- `Content-Type`: Confirms the body is JSON (or tells you it is not, which is a bug worth asserting against).
- `Set-Cookie`: The server sets a session cookie here. In Axios, when `withCredentials: true` is set on an instance, the cookie jar automatically stores this and sends it on subsequent requests. The individual attributes of the cookie (HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite, Expires) are important security properties worth asserting.
- `Content-Length`: The byte length of the body. Useful for detecting truncated responses.
- `ETag`: A hash of the response body, used for caching. Some APIs use this for optimistic concurrency control.

The blank line separates headers from the **response body**. Axios automatically parses a JSON body and places the result in `response.data`. You never call `JSON.parse` manually. If you catch yourself writing `JSON.parse(response.data)`, stop — Axios already did it, and calling it again will throw an error.

In Axios, the full response object looks like:
```typescript
interface AxiosResponse<T = any> {
  data: T;           // parsed JSON body
  status: number;    // 200, 401, etc.
  statusText: string; // "OK", "Unauthorized", etc.
  headers: Record<string, string>; // response headers
  config: AxiosRequestConfig;      // the request config
  request: any;                    // the underlying request object
}
```

You will work primarily with `response.data`, `response.status`, and `response.headers`.

### 2.4 HTTP Methods and Their Semantics

The HTTP method tells the server what kind of operation the client wants to perform. REST APIs use a small set of methods, each with defined semantics.

**GET** retrieves a resource. GET requests are **safe** (they do not modify server state) and **idempotent** (calling the same GET multiple times produces the same result, barring external changes). GET requests have no body. In Chatty: `GET /users/:username/profile` retrieves a user's public profile.

**POST** creates a new resource or triggers a non-idempotent action. POST requests are neither safe nor idempotent — calling POST twice typically creates two resources. POST requests have a body containing the resource to create. In Chatty: `POST /auth/signup` creates a new user, `POST /auth/signin` creates a new session.

**PUT** replaces a resource entirely. If the resource does not exist, PUT may create it (this is implementation-defined). PUT is idempotent — calling PUT with the same body twice produces the same state. Put differently: the result of two identical PUT requests is the same as the result of one. In Chatty, PUT is used sparingly in favor of PATCH.

**PATCH** applies a partial update to a resource. You send only the fields you want to change, not the entire resource. PATCH is not required to be idempotent (though it often is in practice). In Chatty, `PATCH /user/profile` updates specific profile fields without replacing the entire user document.

**DELETE** removes a resource. DELETE is idempotent — deleting an already-deleted resource is not an error in well-designed APIs (though some implementations return 404 on the second call). In Chatty: `DELETE /post/:postId` removes a post.

**Idempotency** deserves special attention in testing. If a test creates a resource (POST), runs some assertions, and then crashes before the cleanup step (DELETE), re-running the test will create a second resource. This is why POST-based test setup needs careful cleanup strategies. GET, PUT, and DELETE-based operations are more forgiving.

**Why Chatty uses PATCH for updates**: Replacing a full user document on every profile update would require the client to send every field — including fields it did not intend to change. This is error-prone and wastes bandwidth. PATCH sends only the diff, which is more efficient and less error-prone. From a testing perspective, PATCH tests must verify both that changed fields are updated and that unchanged fields are preserved.

### 2.5 HTTP Status Codes — A Practical Guide

Status codes are the first thing your tests should check. Understanding the precise semantics of each code makes your assertions more accurate and your test failures more diagnostic.

**200 OK** is the generic success response. The request was received, understood, and processed successfully. Use this as your expected status for GET requests and for PUT/PATCH/DELETE when no new resource was created.

**201 Created** means a new resource was created. It is the correct status code for successful POST requests. Chatty returns 201 from `POST /auth/signup`. The distinction between 200 and 201 matters: asserting `expect(response.status).toBe(201)` tells you that the server specifically acknowledged resource creation, not just that it processed a request without error.

**400 Bad Request** means the client sent something the server could not understand or accept. In Chatty, this typically means Joi validation failed. The response body will include an error message that describes exactly which field failed and why. In tests, you should assert not just the 400 status but the specific error message — this verifies that validation is working correctly and that error messages are user-friendly.

**401 Unauthorized** (the name is a historical misnomer — it really means "unauthenticated") means the request requires authentication that was not provided or was invalid. In Chatty, you receive 401 when you request a protected endpoint without a valid session cookie. After signing out, subsequent requests should return 401. This is a critical security assertion: any endpoint that requires authentication must be tested without credentials to verify the 401.

**403 Forbidden** means the server understood the request and the client is authenticated, but the client does not have permission to perform the operation. In Chatty, you receive 403 when you try to delete another user's post. The distinction between 401 and 403 matters: 401 means "you are not logged in," 403 means "you are logged in but not allowed." Testing both is important for authorization correctness.

**404 Not Found** means the requested resource does not exist. This is the correct response for `GET /users/this-username-does-not-exist` and for `DELETE /post/nonexistent-id`. In tests, you should assert 404 when requesting resources that you know do not exist — including resources you just deleted.

**429 Too Many Requests** means the rate limiter has been triggered. Chatty's API has rate limits to prevent abuse. In tests, you can trigger rate limits if you send too many requests too quickly — for example, in a loop without delays. When your tests start returning 429 responses unexpectedly, the solution is usually to reduce request frequency (use `beforeAll` to make one request per describe block rather than one per test) or to add small delays between requests. In CI/CD, where tests run sequentially, rate limits are rarely an issue. In development, where you may run the same test file repeatedly in quick succession, they can be.

**500 Internal Server Error** means the server encountered an unexpected condition. In your tests, 500 responses always represent bugs — either in the server (a code exception that was not caught) or occasionally in the test (sending malformed data that the server's validation did not catch but that caused downstream errors). When you see 500 in a test, investigate before writing an assertion expecting it. 500s should be extremely rare in a well-tested system.

### 2.6 REST Principles

REST (Representational State Transfer) is an architectural style for distributed hypermedia systems, described by Roy Fielding in his 2000 doctoral dissertation. REST is not a protocol or a specification — it is a set of constraints that, when followed, produce systems with desirable properties.

The six REST constraints:

**Stateless**: Each request must contain all information needed to process it. The server stores no client session state between requests. In Chatty's case, "stateless" applies at the HTTP layer — each request carries a session cookie that identifies the user. The server does not remember anything about previous requests from that client. This matters for testing: you cannot assume that a prior request established any state on the server (beyond what the session cookie and database represent). Each test must be explicit about the state it requires.

**Client-server**: The client and server are separate, with a clean interface between them. The server does not care about the client's UI. The client does not care about the server's database schema. This separation makes API testing possible and valuable — you test the interface, not the implementation.

**Uniform interface**: REST APIs use a consistent interface across all resources. Resources are identified by URLs. Resources are manipulated through representations (JSON). Messages are self-descriptive (Content-Type headers tell you how to interpret the body). This uniformity is why you can transfer patterns between endpoints — learning how one endpoint works teaches you something about all others.

**Layered system**: A client cannot tell whether it is talking directly to the server or to an intermediary (load balancer, reverse proxy, CDN). This enables caching, security, and scalability at the infrastructure level without changing the API contract.

**Cacheable**: Responses should indicate whether they are cacheable. Caching reduces load and improves performance. For testing, you should be aware that CDN caches can serve stale responses — if a test modifies a resource and immediately reads it back, a cached GET may return the old version.

**Code on demand (optional)**: Servers may send executable code (JavaScript) to clients. This constraint is optional and rarely used in REST APIs.

The stateless constraint has the most practical implications for testing. Because the server does not maintain per-client state (beyond what the session cookie identifies), your tests must manage all state explicitly. Before testing an authenticated endpoint, you must sign in and carry the session cookie. Before testing a feature that requires existing data, you must create that data. After the test, you must clean up what you created. We cover state management in detail in Part III.

### 2.7 JSON — The Universal API Language

JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is the standard serialization format for REST APIs. It is a text format derived from JavaScript object literal syntax, designed to be readable by humans and parseable by machines.

**Valid JSON types**: JSON supports six value types. Strings are double-quoted sequences of Unicode characters: `"hello"`, `"user@example.com"`. Numbers are integers or floating-point: `42`, `3.14`, `-7`. Booleans are the literals `true` and `false`. Null is the literal `null`. Arrays are ordered lists of values: `[1, "two", true]`. Objects are unordered collections of key-value pairs, where keys must be strings and values can be any JSON type: `{"name": "Alice", "age": 30}`.

**JSON versus JavaScript objects**: JSON looks like JavaScript object notation but is not identical. In JSON, all keys must be double-quoted strings (JavaScript allows unquoted keys and single-quoted strings). JSON has no `undefined` type (JavaScript does). JSON has no support for functions, symbols, Date objects, or regular expressions. JSON cannot represent circular references. When you serialize a JavaScript object containing `undefined` values, they are silently omitted. This has important implications for testing: asserting that a field is `undefined` in a JSON response is not meaningful — the field will simply not be present.

**How Axios handles JSON**: Axios has built-in JSON handling that removes the need for manual serialization and parsing. When you call `axios.post(url, data)`, Axios:
1. Checks if `data` is a plain object (or array).
2. If so, sets `Content-Type: application/json` automatically.
3. Calls `JSON.stringify(data)` to produce the request body.

When Axios receives a response with `Content-Type: application/json`, it calls `JSON.parse(responseBody)` and assigns the result to `response.data`.

This means you never need to call `JSON.stringify` or `JSON.parse` in test code. `response.data` is always the parsed JavaScript object. This is such an important point that it warrants a rule: **if you find yourself calling `JSON.parse(response.data)` in test code, stop. You are double-parsing.** `response.data` is already a JavaScript object.

**A brief example** of a Chatty API response as a JavaScript object after Axios parsing:
```typescript
// response.data after GET /users/:username/profile
{
  _id: "6612a3b7e2c1d4f0a8b9e123",
  username: "vitest_alice_001",
  email: "alice@example.com",
  profilePicture: "https://res.cloudinary.com/.../profile.jpg",
  postsCount: 3,
  followersCount: 1,
  followingCount: 2,
  blocked: false,
  authId: "6612a3b7e2c1d4f0a8b9e456"
}
```

Every field in this object is a JavaScript value that you can access directly, compare with matchers, and pass to other functions. No parsing required.

**Key Points**

- An HTTP request consists of a method, path, headers, and optionally a body. An HTTP response consists of a status code, headers, and optionally a body.
- Axios auto-serializes request bodies and auto-parses JSON response bodies. `response.data` is always a JavaScript object. Never call `JSON.parse` on it.
- The key methods are GET (safe + idempotent), POST (create), PUT (full replace, idempotent), PATCH (partial update), and DELETE (remove, idempotent).
- Status codes 200, 201, 400, 401, 403, 404, 429, and 500 each have precise semantics. Assert the specific code that the endpoint should return, not just "something in the 2xx range."
- REST's stateless constraint means your tests must manage all state explicitly — authentication, test data creation, and cleanup.
- JSON has six types (string, number, boolean, null, array, object). `undefined` is not a JSON type; fields with undefined values are omitted from serialization.

**Exercises**

1. Using curl on your terminal, make a raw HTTP request to `https://api.codeandtest.com/api/v1/auth/signin` with a JSON body. Use `curl -v` to see both request and response headers. Identify: the request method, the Host header, the Content-Type request header, the response status code, the Content-Type response header, and the Set-Cookie response header. If you do not have curl installed, use the browser's Network tab in DevTools to inspect the same request.

2. The Chatty API returns 401 for unauthenticated requests and 403 for unauthorized requests. Describe in one sentence each: (a) what condition produces a 401, (b) what condition produces a 403, and (c) why the distinction matters for security testing.

3. Consider this statement: "Since Axios sets Content-Type: application/json automatically, I never need to set it manually." Under what circumstances is this statement true? Under what circumstances might it be false? (Hint: think about what data you are sending.)

4. Design a JSON object that represents a chat message in the Chatty application. Include at least six fields with at least four different JSON types. Then identify one field that would be tempting to represent as `undefined` in JavaScript but cannot appear as `undefined` in the JSON response.

5. A test is checking the response from `DELETE /post/:postId`. The developer writes `expect(response.status).toBe(200)`. Is this assertion correct according to REST semantics? What would be a more precise assertion, and why does the distinction matter?

## Chapter 3: Tools of the Trade

Understanding the tools you use is not optional knowledge. When a test fails in an unexpected way — when Axios throws instead of resolving, when TypeScript refuses to compile, when Vitest runs tests in the wrong order — knowing how your tools work is the difference between a five-minute fix and a two-hour debugging session. This chapter explains the tools, the project structure, and the configuration, in enough depth to make you effective.

### 3.1 Why Vitest?

Vitest is a test runner built by the Vite team, first released in 2021. It has rapidly become the preferred test runner for TypeScript and modern JavaScript projects.

**Speed** is the most visible advantage. Vitest uses Vite's native ESM transform pipeline, which means it does not need to compile or bundle test files before running them. A cold start for a large test suite in Vitest typically takes 1–2 seconds. The same suite in Jest often takes 5–15 seconds due to Babel transformation and module caching overhead.

**Native TypeScript support** requires zero configuration in Vitest. You do not need ts-jest, babel-jest, or any other transformation plugin. You write TypeScript, you run Vitest, and it works. Type errors in test files are caught by `tsc --noEmit` in your CI pipeline.

**Identical API to Jest** means that if you have prior Jest experience, you already know most of Vitest. `describe`, `it`, `test`, `expect`, `beforeAll`, `afterAll`, `beforeEach`, `afterEach`, `vi.mock`, `vi.spyOn` — all work identically. Existing Jest guides and StackOverflow answers apply directly to Vitest.

**Built-in coverage** with `@vitest/coverage-v8` requires no additional configuration. `vitest run --coverage` produces coverage reports without a separate tool.

**No globals configuration needed in most setups**, but in our configuration we enable `globals: true` so that `describe`, `it`, `expect`, and hooks are available without imports in test files. This is optional but reduces boilerplate.

### 3.2 Why Axios?

Axios is an HTTP client for Node.js and browsers, built on top of the native `http` module in Node.js and `XMLHttpRequest` in browsers.

**The critical comparison: Axios versus the native `fetch` API**. `fetch` is now available natively in Node.js 18+, so the argument "Axios is easier to use in Node.js" is no longer decisive. The genuine advantages of Axios for test code are:

First, `fetch` throws an error only on network failures (no connection, timeout). It does NOT throw on 4xx or 5xx responses. `fetch` responds with a resolved Promise for any HTTP response, regardless of status code. This seems like what you want for tests — and it is — but `fetch` still requires you to manually call `response.json()` and await it:
```javascript
// fetch approach — two awaits, manual body parsing
const res = await fetch(url, options);
const body = await res.json(); // must manually parse

// Axios approach — one await, body already parsed
const res = await axios.get(url); // res.data is already the object
```

Second, **Axios has `validateStatus`**. This is genuinely important for test code. By default, Axios throws an error for any response with a status code outside 200–299. For tests, this is exactly wrong: you want to test 400s and 401s and 403s without writing try/catch blocks. The `validateStatus: () => true` option disables this behavior, making Axios resolve for any status code. We explore this in detail in Chapter 4. `fetch` does not have an equivalent — it never throws for HTTP status codes.

Third, **Axios instances**. You can create a pre-configured Axios instance with a base URL, default headers, and default options — including `withCredentials: true` for automatic cookie handling. All requests made with that instance inherit these settings. This is cleaner than constructing full URLs and duplicating headers in every `fetch` call.

Fourth, **response object ergonomics**. Axios's `response.data`, `response.status`, `response.headers` are clear, typed properties. `fetch`'s response object requires `.json()`, `.status`, and `.headers.get('content-type')`. For test assertions, Axios's shape is more convenient.

### 3.3 Why TypeScript?

TypeScript adds static type checking to JavaScript. In test code, this pays off in three specific ways.

**Type safety catches shape mismatches before running tests**. If you assert `expect(response.data.userName).toBe('alice')` but the actual property is `response.data.username` (lowercase n), TypeScript catches this at compile time if you have typed the response. Without TypeScript, this test would simply fail with a confusing assertion error.

**Autocomplete for response shapes**. When you define an interface for the expected response shape:
```typescript
interface SigninResponse {
  message: string;
  user: {
    _id: string;
    username: string;
    email: string;
    postsCount: number;
  };
}
```
Your IDE provides autocomplete when you type `response.data.user.` — it lists all available fields. This dramatically speeds up writing assertions.

**`AxiosResponse<T>`** is Axios's generic response type. When you write:
```typescript
const response = await axios.post<SigninResponse>(url, body);
```
`response.data` is typed as `SigninResponse`. Accessing `response.data.user.email` is type-safe. Mistyping `response.data.user.emial` is a compile error.

**TypeScript does not get in the way**. For early exercises, you can use `any` types freely. TypeScript will compile your code without errors. As you become more comfortable, you can add precise types where they help. TypeScript's strictness is adjustable — you do not need 100% type coverage to get value from it.

### 3.4 Project Structure

A well-organized test project makes tests easy to find, easy to run in isolation, and easy to maintain over time. As you work through this book, you will create the following structure — one chapter folder at a time:

```
my-api-tests/
├── src/
│   ├── config.ts        ← load BASE_URL and credentials from .env
│   ├── test-utils.ts    ← shared helpers (expectRejected, expectSuccess)
│   └── fixtures.ts      ← reusable test data (TEST_AVATAR_IMAGE, TEST_PASSWORD)
├── tests/
│   ├── chapter-04/
│   │   └── signin.test.ts
│   ├── chapter-05/
│   │   └── assertions.test.ts
│   ├── chapter-06/
│   │   └── auth.test.ts
│   └── chapter-NN/
│       └── [topic].test.ts
├── .env             ← never committed — contains your credentials
├── .env.example     ← committed — shows required keys without values
├── vitest.config.ts
├── tsconfig.json
└── package.json
```

You only create three files before writing any tests: `src/config.ts`, `src/test-utils.ts`, and `src/fixtures.ts`. Everything else is created chapter by chapter as you progress through the book.

**`src/config.ts`** is the single entry point for all environment configuration. It reads `BASE_URL`, `TEST_USERNAME`, and `TEST_PASSWORD` from your `.env` file and throws a descriptive error if any are missing — rather than letting a test fail with a confusing `undefined` later.

**`src/test-utils.ts`** contains shared helpers used across many test files. The most important is `expectRejected`, a function that accepts status 400 OR 429 as valid rejections — because production auth endpoints can return either depending on rate limiting.

**`src/fixtures.ts`** holds reusable constants. The most important is `TEST_AVATAR_IMAGE`, a base64-encoded 1×1 PNG used for image upload tests. Defining it once here means you never paste a 500-character string into a test file.

**`tests/chapter-NN/`** is where you do your work. Create one test file per chapter, named after the topic — `auth.test.ts`, `posts.test.ts`, `reactions.test.ts`. There is no starter or solution file — you build it from scratch following the exercises in the book.

**`.env`** contains your secrets. It is listed in `.gitignore` and never committed. An `.env.example` is committed instead, showing the required keys with placeholder values so a new developer knows what to set up.

### 3.5 Setting Up the Project

Here is the complete setup from scratch.

**Step 1: Initialize the project**

```bash
mkdir chatty-api-tests
cd chatty-api-tests
npm init -y
```

**Step 2: Install dependencies**

```bash
npm install --save-dev vitest @vitest/coverage-v8 typescript
npm install axios @faker-js/faker dotenv
```

- `vitest` and `@vitest/coverage-v8`: test runner and coverage provider.
- `typescript`: TypeScript compiler.
- `axios`: HTTP client.
- `@faker-js/faker`: Random test data generation (unique usernames, emails, etc.).
- `dotenv`: Loads `.env` files into `process.env`.

**Step 3: Create `tsconfig.json`**

```json
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "target": "ES2022",
    "module": "ESNext",
    "moduleResolution": "bundler",
    "strict": true,
    "esModuleInterop": true,
    "skipLibCheck": true,
    "types": ["vitest/globals"],
    "outDir": "dist",
    "rootDir": "."
  },
  "include": ["src/**/*", "tests/**/*"],
  "exclude": ["node_modules", "dist"]
}
```

The key entry is `"types": ["vitest/globals"]` — this tells TypeScript that `describe`, `it`, `expect`, and the other Vitest globals are defined, so it does not report them as undeclared identifiers.

**Step 4: Create `vitest.config.ts`**

```typescript
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';
import dotenv from 'dotenv';

dotenv.config();

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    globals: true,
    environment: 'node',
    testTimeout: 15000,
    hookTimeout: 30000,
    fileParallelism: false,
    sequence: {
      shuffle: false,
    },
    reporters: ['verbose'],
    env: {
      BASE_URL: process.env.BASE_URL ?? '',
      TEST_USERNAME: process.env.TEST_USERNAME ?? '',
      TEST_PASSWORD: process.env.TEST_PASSWORD ?? '',
      // TEST_CLEANUP_SECRET is hardcoded in src/fixtures.ts — not an env var
    },
  },
});
```

Several of these settings deserve explanation:

`globals: true` makes `describe`, `it`, `expect`, `beforeAll`, etc. available without imports.

`testTimeout: 15000` sets a 15-second timeout per test. API calls typically take 50–500ms, so 15 seconds provides a generous buffer for slow responses without letting broken tests hang indefinitely.

`hookTimeout: 30000` sets a 30-second timeout for `beforeAll` and `afterAll` hooks. Setup and cleanup sometimes need to make several sequential API calls, so they get a longer timeout.

`fileParallelism: false` is the most consequential setting. By default, Vitest runs multiple test files in parallel across worker threads. For unit tests, this is safe and desirable. For API tests against a shared server, it is not. Parallel test files may interfere with each other through shared rate limits, shared test usernames (race conditions on who creates the user first), or shared session state. Setting `fileParallelism: false` makes test files run sequentially. Individual tests within a file still run in the order they are defined, because we want to control the sequence of operations (create before read before delete).

`sequence: { shuffle: false }` ensures tests run in the order they are defined in the file. Test ordering matters when tests build on each other's state.

**Step 5: Create `.env`**

```bash
BASE_URL=https://api.codeandtest.com/api/v1
TEST_USERNAME=your_chatty_username
TEST_PASSWORD=your_chatty_password
# TEST_CLEANUP_SECRET is hardcoded in src/fixtures.ts — do not add to .env
```

**Step 6: Create `.gitignore`**

```
node_modules/
dist/
.env
coverage/
*.log
```

**Step 7: Create `src/config.ts`**

```typescript
import dotenv from 'dotenv';
dotenv.config();

function requireEnv(key: string): string {
  const value = process.env[key];
  if (!value) {
    throw new Error(
      `Missing required environment variable: ${key}. ` +
      `Make sure it is defined in your .env file.`
    );
  }
  return value;
}

export const BASE_URL = requireEnv('BASE_URL');
export const TEST_USERNAME = requireEnv('TEST_USERNAME');
export const TEST_PASSWORD = requireEnv('TEST_PASSWORD');
// TEST_CLEANUP_SECRET is NOT read from env — see src/fixtures.ts
```

**Step 8: Add scripts to `package.json`**

```json
{
  "scripts": {
    "test": "vitest run",
    "test:watch": "vitest",
    "test:coverage": "vitest run --coverage",
    "typecheck": "tsc --noEmit"
  }
}
```

With this setup complete, `npm test` runs all test files once. `npm run test:watch` runs Vitest in watch mode, re-running affected tests on file save. `npm run typecheck` runs the TypeScript compiler without emitting files, catching type errors without running tests.

### 3.6 Environment Variables and Secrets

Never hardcode API URLs, usernames, passwords, or secret keys in test files. This rule has multiple reasons:

**Security**: A hardcoded credential in a test file committed to a public repository is a credential that is compromised. Even in private repositories, keeping credentials out of source code is good practice — it limits blast radius when a repository is accidentally made public or when a developer's machine is compromised.

**Flexibility**: The same test suite should be runnable against multiple environments — development, staging, production. This is only possible if the base URL is configurable. Hardcoding `https://api.codeandtest.com/api/v1` means the tests can only run against production.

**Team practices**: Different team members may have different test accounts. Environment variables allow each developer to use their own credentials without modifying tracked files.

**The `.env` pattern** solves all of these. The `dotenv` library reads a `.env` file from the project root and loads its contents into `process.env` at startup. The file is listed in `.gitignore` so it is never committed. An `.env.example` file is committed instead, containing the same keys with placeholder values, so a new team member knows exactly what variables they need to configure.

The `requireEnv` function in `config.ts` adds a layer of safety: if a required variable is missing, the function throws a clear error message that immediately tells the developer which variable is needed and where to set it. Without this pattern, a missing environment variable produces `undefined` values that fail with confusing type errors deep in test code.

**Why `fileParallelism: false` is essential** for production API testing deserves fuller explanation here. Consider a test suite with three files: `auth.test.ts`, `posts.test.ts`, and `users.test.ts`. With `fileParallelism: true`, all three files start simultaneously in separate worker threads. Now consider:

- All three files need to sign in as the test user. Three concurrent sign-in requests may trigger rate limiting.
- `posts.test.ts` creates a test post. `users.test.ts` queries the same user's post count. Depending on timing, the post count may or may not include the newly created post.
- `auth.test.ts` signs out the test user. Meanwhile, `posts.test.ts`'s `beforeAll` hook is in the middle of signing in.

These race conditions produce intermittent, hard-to-diagnose failures. `fileParallelism: false` eliminates them by ensuring that only one test file runs at a time.

**Key Points**

- Vitest is fast, has native TypeScript support, and has a Jest-compatible API. `fileParallelism: false` is essential for API tests that share server state.
- Axios provides `validateStatus`, automatic JSON parsing, and instance-level configuration. `response.data` is always already parsed — never call `JSON.parse` on it.
- TypeScript's `AxiosResponse<T>` generic provides type-safe access to response bodies. Use it to catch assertion typos at compile time.
- `src/config.ts` with a `requireEnv` function is the right pattern for environment configuration — it fails fast with a clear error if a required variable is missing.
- Never hardcode credentials or API URLs in test files. Always use environment variables loaded from `.env`.
- `fileParallelism: false` prevents race conditions when multiple test files share API state (rate limits, session cookies, test data).

**Exercises**

1. Follow the setup instructions in Section 3.5 to create the project structure from scratch. Verify that `npm test` runs without errors on an empty test directory.

2. Create `src/config.ts` with the `requireEnv` pattern. Write a test (in a separate scratch file, not in the `tests/` directory) that imports `BASE_URL` from `config.ts` and asserts that it is a string starting with `https://`. Run it with `npm test`.

3. Deliberately break the setup by removing `BASE_URL` from your `.env` file and running `npm test`. Document the error message you receive. Restore the variable. This exercise teaches you what the `requireEnv` guard looks like when it triggers.

4. Open `vitest.config.ts` and temporarily set `fileParallelism: true`. Create two test files that both `console.log('started')` in their `beforeAll` hooks and `console.log('finished')` in their `afterAll` hooks, with a 500ms delay (`await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 500))`) in each hook. Run `npm test` and observe the interleaved output. Then restore `fileParallelism: false` and observe the sequential output. This exercise makes the parallelism difference concrete.

5. The `vitest.config.ts` shown in Section 3.5 sets `testTimeout: 15000`. What happens if a test makes an API call and the server takes 20 seconds to respond? Write a test that artificially waits 16 seconds (using `setTimeout`) and observe Vitest's timeout error message. Then change the timeout to 20 seconds and observe that the test now passes. Restore the timeout to 15 seconds.

Suggested project structure for this chapter's exercises:

```
tests/chapter-03/

```

Write these tests in your file before reading the next chapter:

2. Create src/config.ts that reads BASE_URL, TEST_USERNAME, and TEST_PASSWORD from environment variables and throws a descriptive error if any are missing.
3. Create src/test-utils.ts with an expectRejected function that accepts status 400 OR 429.
4. Create src/fixtures.ts with TEST_PASSWORD and a TEST_AVATAR_IMAGE constant (a 1x1 PNG as a base64 data URL).
5. Write a single test file that imports from all three src/ files and makes one request to POST /signin. Run it with npm test. The test should pass.

### 3.7 Discovering the API — Live References

Before writing a test for an endpoint you haven't used before, check what fields it accepts and what errors it returns. The Chatty API provides two live references that always reflect the current deployed version:

**Swagger UI — interactive browser docs**
```
https://api.codeandtest.com/api-docs
```
Browse every endpoint, see its request body schema, send test requests from the browser, and read the exact response shape. When you are unsure whether a field is required or what its validation constraints are, this is the first place to look.

**Schema endpoint — machine-readable validation rules**
```
GET https://api.codeandtest.com/api/v1/schema
```
Returns a JSON object listing every endpoint with its fields, types, min/max constraints, required status, success response shape, and all possible error messages. Useful when tests start failing after a deployment and you want to check whether a validation rule changed.

```bash
curl https://api.codeandtest.com/api/v1/schema | jq '.endpoints[] | select(.path == "/api/v1/signup")'
```

Both references update automatically when the backend is deployed — you never need to ask whether the documentation is current.

# Part II: Writing Your First Tests

---

## Chapter 4: The Anatomy of an API Test

You now have the conceptual foundation and the tooling setup. It is time to write tests. This chapter introduces the fundamental structure of an API test file — the patterns you will use in every test file you write for the rest of this book and throughout your career.

### 4.1 The Four Phases

Every automated test, regardless of what it tests, has four phases. These phases are sometimes called AAA (Arrange-Act-Assert) or, with the addition of cleanup, AACL (Arrange-Act-Assert-Cleanup). In API testing, they map directly to Vitest's lifecycle hooks.

**Arrange** is the setup phase. You put the system into the state required for the test. For an API test, this typically means: ensure the required user account exists, sign in to obtain a session, create any test data the test will operate on. Arrangement happens in `beforeAll` hooks.

**Act** is the action phase. You perform the operation under test — make the HTTP request. In most of our test files, the Act phase happens in `beforeAll` as well: one request is made, and its response is stored in a shared variable that all tests in the describe block can read.

**Assert** is the verification phase. You check that the response is correct. Each `it` block typically contains one focused assertion (or a small group of closely related assertions) against the response captured in the Act phase.

**Cleanup** is the teardown phase. You restore the system to the state it was in before the test. For API tests, this means: delete created resources, sign out sessions, clean up test users. Cleanup happens in `afterAll` hooks.

Here is the skeleton of a well-structured API test file:

```typescript
import axios, { AxiosResponse } from 'axios';
import { BASE_URL } from '../../src/config';

describe('POST /auth/signin', () => {
  // Arrange: the user exists (assumed in this example)
  let response!: AxiosResponse;

  beforeAll(async () => {
    // Act: make the HTTP request once
    response = await axios.post(
      `${BASE_URL}/auth/signin`,
      { username: 'testuser', password: 'password123' },
      { validateStatus: () => true }
    );
  });

  // Assert: each test reads from the shared response
  describe('1. Basic', () => {
    it('returns 200 status code', () => {
      expect(response.status).toBe(200);
    });
  });

  describe('2. Response shape', () => {
    it('has a message field', () => {
      expect(response.data).toHaveProperty('message');
    });

    it('has a user object', () => {
      expect(response.data).toHaveProperty('user');
    });
  });

  // Cleanup happens in afterAll
  afterAll(async () => {
    // sign out, clean up test data if needed
  });
});
```

The lifecycle and data flow are: `beforeAll` runs once before any `it` blocks, performs the request, stores the result. Each `it` block runs afterward and reads from `response`. `afterAll` runs once after all `it` blocks.

### 4.2 Your First Test — The Wrong Way

Before showing the right pattern, it is worth understanding the wrong pattern — not as a curiosity, but because you will encounter this mistake in real codebases and need to recognize it.

Here is a test file that makes the same sign-in request in every test:

```typescript
// ANTI-PATTERN: Don't do this
import axios from 'axios';
import { BASE_URL } from '../../src/config';

describe('POST /auth/signin', () => {
  it('returns 200 status code', async () => {
    const response = await axios.post(
      `${BASE_URL}/auth/signin`,
      { username: 'testuser', password: 'password123' },
      { validateStatus: () => true }
    );
    expect(response.status).toBe(200);
  });

  it('returns a message', async () => {
    const response = await axios.post(
      `${BASE_URL}/auth/signin`,
      { username: 'testuser', password: 'password123' },
      { validateStatus: () => true }
    );
    expect(response.data.message).toBeDefined();
  });

  it('returns a user object', async () => {
    const response = await axios.post(
      `${BASE_URL}/auth/signin`,
      { username: 'testuser', password: 'password123' },
      { validateStatus: () => true }
    );
    expect(response.data.user).toBeDefined();
  });

  // ... 7 more tests, each making the same request
});
```

This approach has several problems:

**Excessive requests**: If this describe block has 10 tests, it makes 10 sign-in requests. This is ten times slower than it needs to be. At 200ms per request, that is 2 seconds wasted in a single describe block. At scale — hundreds of describe blocks — this becomes minutes.

**Rate limiting risk**: Many production APIs rate-limit repeated identical requests. Ten rapid sign-in requests from the same IP address may trigger the rate limiter, causing tests 7–10 to return 429 instead of 200. The tests fail, but for the wrong reason.

**Inconsistency**: If the server state changes between test 1 and test 3 (unlikely for sign-in, but very relevant for endpoints that modify data), different tests may see different responses.

**Wasteful duplication**: Every test function contains the same boilerplate request setup. If the endpoint URL changes, you must update ten places instead of one.

### 4.3 Your First Test — The Right Way

The correct pattern makes one request in `beforeAll` and tests all aspects of that single response:

```typescript
import axios, { AxiosResponse } from 'axios';
import { BASE_URL, TEST_USERNAME, TEST_PASSWORD } from '../../src/config';

describe('POST /auth/signin - success', () => {
  let response!: AxiosResponse;

  beforeAll(async () => {
    response = await axios.post(
      `${BASE_URL}/auth/signin`,
      {
        username: TEST_USERNAME,
        password: TEST_PASSWORD,
      },
      {
        validateStatus: () => true,
      }
    );
  });

  describe('1. Basic', () => {
    it('returns 200 status code', () => {
      expect(response.status).toBe(200);
    });
  });

  describe('2. Exact values', () => {
    it('returns success message', () => {
      expect(response.data.message).toBe('User login successfully');
    });
  });

  describe('3. Shape', () => {
    it('has a user object with required fields', () => {
      expect(response.data.user).toMatchObject({
        username: expect.any(String),
        email: expect.any(String),
        _id: expect.any(String),
      });
    });
  });

  describe('4. Security', () => {
    it('does not expose password hash', () => {
      expect(response.data.user).not.toHaveProperty('password');
    });
  });
});
```

This version makes exactly **one** HTTP request. All tests in the describe block read from the shared `response` variable. Request count goes from 10 to 1. Rate limit risk goes to zero. All tests see exactly the same response object.

The `let response!: AxiosResponse` declaration warrants explanation. `let` because we will assign it in `beforeAll`, not at declaration time. `AxiosResponse` is the type. The `!` is TypeScript's non-null assertion operator. Without it, TypeScript would complain that `response` is used before being assigned (it is assigned in `beforeAll`, not at the `let` statement). The `!` tells TypeScript: "I know this will be assigned before use." This is a standard pattern in Vitest test files.

### 4.4 validateStatus: () => true

This option deserves its own section because it is one of the most important and least intuitive aspects of using Axios for testing.

By default, Axios throws an error (rejects the Promise) for any response with a status code outside the 200–299 range. This means:

```typescript
// WITHOUT validateStatus
const response = await axios.post(url, { username: '', password: '' });
// If the server returns 400, Axios THROWS here.
// The code below never runs.
console.log(response.status); // never reached
```

This default behavior is sensible for application code: in a production app, you usually want errors to propagate automatically. But for tests, it is exactly wrong. Tests need to inspect 400, 401, 403, 404, 429, and 500 responses. If Axios throws for 4xx responses, you either have to wrap every test request in a try/catch block:

```typescript
// AWKWARD: try/catch for every test
it('returns 400 for missing username', async () => {
  let response;
  try {
    response = await axios.post(url, { password: 'x' });
  } catch (error: any) {
    response = error.response;
  }
  expect(response.status).toBe(400);
});
```

This is ugly, verbose, and fragile. If the request fails with a network error (not an HTTP error), `error.response` will be undefined and your test fails with a confusing null-pointer error.

The clean solution is `validateStatus: () => true`:

```typescript
// CLEAN: validateStatus: () => true
const response = await axios.post(url, body, {
  validateStatus: () => true, // never throw for any status code
});
// response is always defined here, for any status code
expect(response.status).toBe(400);
```

The `() => true` is a function that Axios calls with the status code and returns `true` if the response is considered valid (i.e., should resolve rather than reject). By always returning `true`, we tell Axios: every status code is valid, always resolve.

You can also configure this on an Axios instance, so you do not need to repeat it on every request:

```typescript
import axios from 'axios';
import { BASE_URL } from './src/config';

export const api = axios.create({
  baseURL: BASE_URL,
  validateStatus: () => true,
  withCredentials: true,
});
```

With this shared instance, every request you make with `api.get(...)`, `api.post(...)`, etc. automatically has `validateStatus: () => true` and `withCredentials: true`.

### 4.5 The describe Block

The `describe` function creates a named group of tests. Describes can be nested. Nesting creates a tree of test names that Vitest displays in its output:

```
POST /auth/signin - success
  1. Basic
    ✓ returns 200 status code
  2. Exact values
    ✓ returns success message "User login successfully"
  3. Shape
    ✓ user object contains _id, username, email
  4. Security
    ✓ does not expose password hash
```

The numbered section pattern (1. Basic, 2. Exact values, 3. Shape, 4. Negative, 5. Boundary, 6. Headers) is a convention that produces readable output and encourages thorough coverage. You are not required to use this exact pattern, but you should organize tests into logical groups.

Nested `beforeAll` hooks work at the level of their enclosing `describe` block. An outer `describe`'s `beforeAll` runs before all inner `describe` blocks. An inner `describe`'s `beforeAll` runs only before the tests in that inner `describe`. This allows you to structure complex test files with shared setup at the outer level and more specific setup at the inner level.

### 4.6 async/await in Tests

Vitest test functions (and lifecycle hooks) can be either synchronous or asynchronous. If your test function is async (returns a Promise), Vitest awaits it before proceeding to the next test.

The async/await style is the correct choice for tests that make HTTP requests:

```typescript
it('returns 200 status code', async () => {
  const response = await axios.get(url, { validateStatus: () => true });
  expect(response.status).toBe(200);
});
```

There is an older pattern using `.then()`. Using `.then()` in tests requires you to **return the Promise**, or Vitest will not wait for your assertions:

```typescript
// DANGEROUS: if you forget to return, the test always passes
it('returns 200 status code', () => {
  // MISSING return — this test will ALWAYS pass silently
  axios.get(url, { validateStatus: () => true }).then(response => {
    expect(response.status).toBe(200);
  });
});

// CORRECT with .then(): must return the Promise
it('returns 200 status code', () => {
  return axios.get(url, { validateStatus: () => true }).then(response => {
    expect(response.status).toBe(200);
  });
});
```

The test without `return` is an extremely common source of false positives: the test appears to pass because Vitest completes it before the Promise resolves, and by the time the assertion runs, Vitest has moved on. The assertion failure is silently swallowed.

Async/await eliminates this hazard. **Always use async/await in test functions that make HTTP calls.** The only exception is tests that do not do any async work (like assertions on values already computed in `beforeAll`), which can be synchronous:

```typescript
// No async work needed — response already computed in beforeAll
it('returns 200 status code', () => {
  expect(response.status).toBe(200);
});
```

### 4.7 Test Naming

A test name should read as a complete statement describing the expected behavior. The format `when [condition], [expected outcome]` or `[action] [expected result]` works well.

Compare:

```typescript
// POOR test names
it('status code', ...) // What status code? Pass or fail?
it('test1', ...)       // Meaningless
it('works', ...)       // Works how?

// GOOD test names
it('returns 200 when credentials are valid', ...)
it('returns 401 when credentials are missing', ...)
it('returns 401 when password is incorrect', ...)
it('does not expose password hash in response', ...)
it('includes set-cookie header with session token', ...)
it('user._id is a non-empty string', ...)
```

Good test names serve as living documentation. When you run the test suite and see this output:

```
POST /auth/signin
  Success path
    ✓ returns 200 when credentials are valid
    ✓ does not expose password hash in response
  Failure path
    ✓ returns 401 when credentials are missing
    ✓ returns 401 when password is incorrect
    ✓ returns 400 when username is empty string
```

You can read this as a specification of the endpoint's behavior. A new team member reading this output understands what the endpoint is supposed to do before reading a single line of source code.

When a test fails, a good test name tells you immediately what behavior broke:
```
✗ returns 200 when credentials are valid
```
versus:
```
✗ test1
```

The first tells you the sign-in success path is broken. The second tells you nothing.

**Key Points**

- Every API test has four phases: Arrange (beforeAll: setup), Act (beforeAll: make request), Assert (it blocks: check response), Cleanup (afterAll: teardown).
- The `beforeAll` pattern — one request, many tests — is fundamental. It reduces request count, eliminates rate limit risk, and ensures all tests in a describe block see the same response.
- `validateStatus: () => true` tells Axios never to throw for any HTTP status code. This is essential for testing 4xx and 5xx responses without try/catch blocks.
- Always use async/await in test functions. Never use `.then()` without returning the Promise — the assertion will silently be swallowed.
- `let response!: AxiosResponse` with the `!` non-null assertion is the standard TypeScript pattern for variables assigned in `beforeAll`.
- Test names should read as complete behavioral specifications. They are living documentation.

**Exercises**

Write a test file at `tests/lecture-04/lecture.test.ts` that tests `POST /auth/signin` at `https://api.codeandtest.com/api/v1`. Your file should:

1. Use the `beforeAll` pattern with one request shared across all tests.
2. Assert the status code is 200.
3. Assert that `response.data.message` is defined and is a string.
4. Assert that `response.data.user` is an object.
5. Assert that `response.data.user.username` equals your test username.

After your tests pass, add a second `describe` block for the failure case: send a request with an incorrect password. In `beforeAll`, make one request with a wrong password. Assert that the status code is 401. Assert that `response.data.message` is defined. Assert that `response.data` does NOT contain a `user` property.
