## The Test File for This Chapter

> **Lecture 01 — Setup & First API Test**
> Run: `npm test tests/lecture-01/lecture.test.ts`

```ts
// Lecture 01 — Setup & First API Test
//
// Endpoint tested: POST /api/v1/signin (with wrong/invalid credentials)
//
// This file demonstrates SIX categories of assertions you can write:
//   1. Basic assertions         — status code, body field existence
//   2. Exact value assertions   — assert what the value IS, not just that it exists
//   3. One request, many checks — make ONE request, run many assertions on it
//   4. Shape validation         — assert the entire response structure at once
//   5. Negative assertions      — assert what should NOT be in the response
//   6. Boundary value tests     — test the edges of the Joi validation schema
//   7. Header assertions        — check response headers
//   8. Response time            — performance assertion
//
// IMPORTANT — rate limiting:
//   The production server allows 5 requests/minute on /signin (nginx) +
//   20 requests / 15 minutes (Express).
//   To stay well under this limit, sections 1–5 and 7–8 share ONE HTTP request
//   made in the top-level beforeAll below.
//   Only section 6 (boundary tests) makes individual requests.
//
// Signin Joi schema (from chatty-backend/src/features/auth/schemas/signin.ts):
//   username: string, required, min 4, max 32
//   password: string, required, min 8, max 128
//
// Run: npm test tests/lecture-01/lecture.test.ts

import axios, { type AxiosResponse } from 'axios';
import { config } from '../../src/config';
import { expectRejected } from '../../src/test-utils';

const url = `${config.BASE_URL}/signin`;

const wrongCredentials = {
  username: 'notarealuser99999',
  password: 'WrongPass@9999',
};

// ─── File-level shared request ────────────────────────────────────────────────
//
// ONE HTTP request shared across sections 1–5, 7, and 8.
// This is the efficient pattern: make as few network calls as possible.
// All assertions in those sections read from this single response object.
//
// beforeAll() at the file root (outside any describe) runs ONCE
// before any test in the entire file.

let sharedResponse!: AxiosResponse;

beforeAll(async () => {
  sharedResponse = await axios.post(url, wrongCredentials, {
    validateStatus: () => true,
  });
});

// ─── Rate limit note ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
//
// expectRejected() is imported from src/test-utils.ts — see STANDARDS.md §5.
// It accepts status 400 (validation error) OR 429 (rate limited) as valid rejections.

// ─── 1. Basic assertions ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
//
// The simplest form: check that a field exists, check the status code.
// These tests read from `sharedResponse` — no extra network call needed.

describe('1. Basic assertions', () => {

  it('returns status 400 for wrong credentials', () => {
    expectRejected(sharedResponse.status);
  });

  it('response body has a message field', () => {
    // toHaveProperty checks the key exists — does not check the value
    expect(sharedResponse.data).toHaveProperty('message');
  });

  it('response body has a status field', () => {
    if (sharedResponse.status === 429) return; // 429 response has no status field
    expect(sharedResponse.data).toHaveProperty('status');
  });

});

// ─── 2. Exact value assertions ────────────────────────────────────────────────
//
// Always assert WHAT the value is, not just that it exists.
// .toHaveProperty('message') tells you the key exists.
// .toBe('Invalid credentials') tells you the actual value is correct.
// Both are needed. Existence check alone is too weak.

describe('2. Exact value assertions', () => {

  it('message is exactly "Invalid credentials"', () => {
    // Guard: 429 responses have a different message — skip the value check
    if (sharedResponse.status === 429) return;
    expect(sharedResponse.data.message).toBe('Invalid credentials');
  });

  it('statusCode inside body matches HTTP status', () => {
    if (sharedResponse.status === 429) return;
    // The Chatty API echoes the HTTP status code inside the JSON body too.
    // response.status        → HTTP status code (from the network response)
    // response.data.statusCode → status code repeated inside the JSON body
    // Both should match. They come from different places.
    expect(sharedResponse.data.statusCode).toBe(sharedResponse.status);
  });

  it('message is a non-empty string', () => {
    // typeof check confirms it is a string (not a number, object, etc.)
    expect(typeof sharedResponse.data.message).toBe('string');
    // Length check confirms it is not an empty string
    expect(sharedResponse.data.message.length).toBeGreaterThan(0);
  });

});

// ─── 3. One request, many checks ─────────────────────────────────────────────
//
// The pattern: make ONE request, run multiple assertions on it.
// This is already what we are doing here with sharedResponse.
// Contrast with sections 1 and 2 above — there we described the concept.
// Here we show it explicitly with no beforeAll (the file-level one handles it).

describe('3. One request, many checks — demonstrated', () => {

  it('all fields are correct in one assertion each', () => {
    // All of these read from the SAME single HTTP request
    expectRejected(sharedResponse.status);
    expect(sharedResponse.data).toHaveProperty('message');
    expect(typeof sharedResponse.data.message).toBe('string');
    expect(sharedResponse.data.message.length).toBeGreaterThan(0);
  });

});

// ─── 4. Shape validation with toMatchObject ───────────────────────────────────
//
// Assert the ENTIRE response structure in one assertion instead of field by field.
// toMatchObject checks that the object contains at least the specified keys/values.
// Extra keys in the response are allowed — only specified ones are checked.
//
// expect.any(Type) — checks the value is an instance of Type, not its exact value.
// Use when you know the type but the value can vary.

describe('4. Shape validation', () => {

  it('response body matches the expected error shape', () => {
    if (sharedResponse.status === 429) {
      // 429 response only has { message } — skip full shape check
      expect(sharedResponse.data).toHaveProperty('message');
      return;
    }

    expect(sharedResponse.data).toMatchObject({
      message: expect.any(String),    // any string value
      status: 'error',                // exact value
      statusCode: expect.any(Number), // any number value
    });
  });

  it('all three error fields have the right types', () => {
    if (sharedResponse.status === 429) return;

    expect(typeof sharedResponse.data.message).toBe('string');
    expect(typeof sharedResponse.data.status).toBe('string');
    expect(typeof sharedResponse.data.statusCode).toBe('number');
  });

});

// ─── 5. Negative assertions — what should NOT be there ───────────────────────
//
// Checking what IS in the response is only half the job.
// Checking what is NOT there is equally important — especially for security.
// Use .not to negate any matcher.

describe('5. Negative assertions', () => {

  it('response does not expose a password field', () => {
    // Security: a server must never return a password in any response
    expect(sharedResponse.data).not.toHaveProperty('password');
  });

  it('response does not include a token on failed login', () => {
    // A JWT token should only be returned on SUCCESSFUL login
    expect(sharedResponse.data).not.toHaveProperty('token');
  });

  it('response does not include a user object on failed login', () => {
    // User data should only be returned after successful authentication
    expect(sharedResponse.data).not.toHaveProperty('user');
  });

  it('status is not 200 or 201 (not a false success)', () => {
    // The server must never return a success code for invalid credentials
    expect(sharedResponse.status).not.toBe(200);
    expect(sharedResponse.status).not.toBe(201);
  });

});

// ─── 6. Boundary value tests ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
//
// Boundary value analysis: test the exact edges of the validation rules.
// Schema: username min 4 / max 32, password min 8 / max 128.
//
// These tests MUST make individual requests (each has different input).
// They use expectRejected() to handle both 400 (validation error) and 429 (rate limit).
// The message check is conditional on receiving a 400 (not a rate-limited 429).
//
// TIP: run this file against localhost (no rate limiter) for clean 400 responses.

describe('6. Boundary value tests — Joi schema limits', () => {

  it('username shorter than 4 chars is rejected', async () => {
    const res = await axios.post(
      url,
      { username: 'abc', password: 'ValidPass@1' }, // 3 chars — below min 4
      { validateStatus: () => true },
    );

    expectRejected(res.status);
    if (res.status === 400) {
      expect(res.data.message).toContain('Invalid username');
    }
  });

  it('username longer than 32 chars is rejected', async () => {
    const res = await axios.post(
      url,
      { username: 'a'.repeat(33), password: 'ValidPass@1' }, // 33 chars — above max 32
      { validateStatus: () => true },
    );

    expectRejected(res.status);
    if (res.status === 400) {
      expect(res.data.message).toContain('Invalid username');
    }
  });

  it('password shorter than 8 chars is rejected', async () => {
    const res = await axios.post(
      url,
      { username: 'validuser', password: 'Pass@1!' }, // 7 chars — below min 8
      { validateStatus: () => true },
    );

    expectRejected(res.status);
    if (res.status === 400) {
      expect(res.data.message).toContain('Invalid password');
    }
  });

  it('password longer than 128 chars is rejected', async () => {
    const res = await axios.post(
      url,
      { username: 'validuser', password: 'A@1' + 'a'.repeat(127) }, // 130 chars
      { validateStatus: () => true },
    );

    expectRejected(res.status);
    if (res.status === 400) {
      expect(res.data.message).toContain('Invalid password');
    }
  });

  it('missing username is rejected', async () => {
    const res = await axios.post(
      url,
      { password: 'ValidPass@1' }, // no username field
      { validateStatus: () => true },
    );

    expectRejected(res.status);
    if (res.status === 400) {
      // Joi distinction:
      //   Field absent entirely → 'any.required' → '"username" is required' (Joi default)
      //   Field present + empty → 'string.empty'  → 'Username is a required field' (custom)
      expect(res.data.message).toContain('"username" is required');
    }
  });

  it('missing password is rejected', async () => {
    const res = await axios.post(
      url,
      { username: 'validuser' }, // no password field
      { validateStatus: () => true },
    );

    expectRejected(res.status);
    if (res.status === 400) {
      expect(res.data.message).toContain('"password" is required');
    }
  });

  it('completely empty body is rejected', async () => {
    const res = await axios.post(url, {}, { validateStatus: () => true });
    expectRejected(res.status);
  });

});

// ─── 7. Header assertions ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
//
// Response headers carry important metadata.
// Content-Type tells you the format of the body.
// Always check it — if a server returns HTML instead of JSON by mistake,
// this assertion will catch it immediately.

describe('7. Header assertions', () => {

  it('Content-Type is application/json', () => {
    // Full value: "application/json; charset=utf-8"
    // toContain checks for substring — needed because of the "; charset=utf-8" suffix
    expect(sharedResponse.headers['content-type']).toContain('application/json');
  });

  it('response declares its body size', () => {
    // Server must indicate body size via content-length or transfer-encoding
    const hasContentLength = 'content-length' in sharedResponse.headers;
    const hasTransferEncoding = 'transfer-encoding' in sharedResponse.headers;
    expect(hasContentLength || hasTransferEncoding).toBe(true);
  });

});

// ─── 8. Response time ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
//
// API responses should arrive quickly. Slow responses indicate:
//   - A missing database index (query scans the full collection)
//   - An N+1 query problem
//   - Blocking synchronous code on the server
//
// The file-level beforeAll already measured the time for sharedResponse,
// so we measure a fresh request here for an isolated timing.

describe('8. Response time', () => {

  it('responds within 3000ms', async () => {
    const start = Date.now();
    await axios.post(url, wrongCredentials, { validateStatus: () => true });
    const duration = Date.now() - start;

    expect(duration).toBeLessThan(3000);
  });

});

// ─── 9. Assertion variants ────────────────────────────────────────────────────
//
// Three assertion types not used elsewhere in this file:
//   toMatch(/regex/)     — assert a string matches a regular expression pattern
//   toBeTypeOf('string') — Vitest-native type check, cleaner than `typeof x === '...'`
//   toBeTruthy / toBeFalsy — loose truthiness check, no strict equality needed
//
// All read from sharedResponse — no extra HTTP call.

describe('9. Assertion variants', () => {

  it('message matches a non-empty string pattern', () => {
    // toMatch accepts a regex — useful for asserting format without knowing exact value.
    // /\S+/ means "one or more non-whitespace characters" — any non-blank string passes.
    expect(sharedResponse.data.message).toMatch(/\S+/);
  });

  it('statusCode is of type number — toBeTypeOf', () => {
    if (sharedResponse.status === 429) return; // 429 response has no statusCode field
    // toBeTypeOf is Vitest-specific — cleaner than `expect(typeof x).toBe('number')`.
    // It reads like a sentence and gives a better failure message.
    expect(sharedResponse.data.statusCode).toBeTypeOf('number');
  });

  it('message is truthy', () => {
    // toBeTruthy passes for any value that is not: false, 0, '', null, undefined, NaN.
    // A non-empty string is always truthy — this confirms the field is populated.
    expect(sharedResponse.data.message).toBeTruthy();
  });

  it('response body has no token — toBeFalsy on presence check', () => {
    // Alternative to .not.toHaveProperty — compute the boolean, then assert it is falsy.
    // toBeFalsy passes for false, 0, '', null, undefined — all mean "not present".
    const hasToken = 'token' in sharedResponse.data;
    expect(hasToken).toBeFalsy();
  });

});
```

## Chapter 5: Assertions — Checking What Matters

Assertions are the core of a test. The `expect()` API is where you translate your understanding of correct behavior into code. Vitest's assertion library is rich and expressive — there is a matcher for nearly every situation. This chapter is a comprehensive guide to the matchers you will use most, with examples drawn from real Chatty API responses.

### 5.1 The Philosophy of Assertions

There is a spectrum of assertion strategies, and both extremes are wrong.

At one extreme: **assert nothing but the status code**. This is common in beginner tests and produces tests that pass even when the response body is complete garbage. A test that only checks `response.status === 200` will pass even if the response body is `{ error: "something went wrong" }` with status 200 (which does happen with some poorly designed APIs).

At the other extreme: **assert the entire response body as an exact match**. This produces tests that break on every non-breaking change. If you assert the exact value of a timestamp, tests fail whenever the timestamp changes (which is every time the resource is modified). If you assert the exact list of fields in a response, tests fail when the API adds a new optional field (which is a non-breaking change).

The right approach is in the middle: **assert what you care about**. Ask: "If this assertion fails, does it indicate a real bug?" If yes, keep the assertion. If the assertion would break due to an unrelated change (a different user's data changing, an optional field being added, a timestamp changing), the assertion is too brittle.

Practically, this means:
- Assert exact status codes (200 vs 201 vs 400).
- Assert exact values for stable, deterministic data (a specific user's username, a constant message string).
- Assert types and shapes for dynamic data (a new resource's `_id` is a string, a list of posts has the right shape).
- Assert absence for security-sensitive fields (password must not be present).
- Assert relationships for computed fields (postsCount equals the number of posts you created).
- Avoid asserting timestamps, ordering of unordered arrays, or computed values that change independently of the behavior under test.

### 5.2 The Complete Matcher Guide

#### Equality Matchers

**`toBe(value)`** uses strict equality (`===`). It is correct for primitive values: numbers, strings, booleans, null. It is wrong for objects and arrays — two objects with the same structure are not `===` equal in JavaScript.

```typescript
expect(response.status).toBe(200);              // correct: number
expect(response.data.message).toBe('User login successfully'); // correct: string
expect(response.data.user.verified).toBe(true); // correct: boolean

// WRONG: objects are never === equal unless they are the same reference
expect(response.data.user).toBe({ _id: '...', username: '...' }); // always fails
```

**`toEqual(value)`** performs a deep equality check. Two objects are `toEqual` equal if they have the same structure and values recursively. This is the right matcher for objects and arrays.

```typescript
expect(response.data.user).toEqual({
  _id: '6612a3b7e2c1d4f0a8b9e123',
  username: 'vitest_alice_001',
  email: 'alice@example.com',
  postsCount: 0,
  followersCount: 0,
  followingCount: 0,
});
```

Note that `toEqual` ignores `undefined` properties (fields with value `undefined` are treated as absent). This is usually what you want for JSON comparison, since JSON does not have `undefined`.

**`toStrictEqual(value)`** is like `toEqual` but also checks for `undefined` properties and object types. Use this when you need to distinguish `{ a: undefined }` from `{}`, or when you need to distinguish a plain object from a class instance. In practice, `toEqual` is almost always sufficient for API response assertions.

When to use which:
- Status codes, counts, booleans: `toBe`
- Constant message strings: `toBe`
- Full response body comparison: `toEqual`
- Partial object matching (see below): `toMatchObject`

#### String Matchers

**`toContain(substring)`** checks that a string contains the given substring. Useful for checking error messages that may include variable content:

```typescript
expect(response.data.message).toContain('required');
// passes for "Username is required" and "Password is required"
// more flexible than toBe
```

**`toMatch(regexp)`** checks a string against a regular expression. Use this for format validation when `toContain` is not specific enough:

```typescript
// JWT format: three base64url segments separated by dots
expect(response.headers['set-cookie'][0]).toMatch(
  /session=[A-Za-z0-9\-_]+\.[A-Za-z0-9\-_]+\.[A-Za-z0-9\-_]+/
);

// MongoDB ObjectId: 24 hex characters
expect(response.data.user._id).toMatch(/^[0-9a-f]{24}$/);

// Cloudinary URL
expect(response.data.user.profilePicture).toMatch(
  /^https:\/\/res\.cloudinary\.com\//
);
```

**`expect.stringContaining(substring)`** is an asymmetric matcher — it is used inside `toEqual` or `toMatchObject` to check that a field contains a substring, without requiring an exact value for the whole object:

```typescript
expect(response.data).toMatchObject({
  message: expect.stringContaining('successfully'),
  user: expect.objectContaining({ username: 'vitest_alice_001' }),
});
```

#### Number Matchers

**`toBeGreaterThan(n)`**, **`toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(n)`**, **`toBeLessThan(n)`**, **`toBeLessThanOrEqual(n)`** are for numeric range assertions:

```typescript
expect(response.data.user.postsCount).toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(0);
expect(response.data.posts.length).toBeLessThanOrEqual(10); // page size check
expect(responseTimeMs).toBeLessThan(2000); // performance assertion
```

These matchers are particularly valuable for counts, list lengths, and timestamps:

```typescript
const now = Date.now();
const createdAt = new Date(response.data.post.createdAt).getTime();
expect(createdAt).toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(now - 5000); // within 5 seconds of now
expect(createdAt).toBeLessThanOrEqual(now + 1000);    // not in the future
```

#### Existence Matchers

**`toBeDefined()`** asserts that the value is not `undefined`. Use this when you do not know or do not care about the exact value, but want to confirm the field exists:

```typescript
expect(response.data.user._id).toBeDefined();
expect(response.data.user.email).toBeDefined();
```

**`toBeNull()`** asserts strict `null`. In JavaScript, `null` and `undefined` are different things. Use `toBeNull()` when the API should return `null` for a missing optional value (rather than omitting the field entirely):

```typescript
// profilePicture is null for users who have not uploaded one
expect(response.data.user.profilePicture).toBeNull();
```

**`toBeTruthy()`** asserts that the value is truthy — any value other than `false`, `0`, `''`, `null`, `undefined`, and `NaN`. Use sparingly; it is too loose for most API assertions:

```typescript
// Acceptable: the message is a non-empty string, but we don't care about its exact value
expect(response.data.message).toBeTruthy();

// Better: if you know the message, assert it exactly
expect(response.data.message).toBe('User login successfully');
```

**`toBeFalsy()`** asserts falsy. Useful for boolean flags:

```typescript
expect(response.data.user.blocked).toBeFalsy(); // user is not blocked
```

#### Type Checking

**`toBeTypeOf('string')`** is Vitest's clean type-checking matcher. It is equivalent to `typeof value === 'string'` but produces a better error message:

```typescript
expect(response.data.user._id).toBeTypeOf('string');
expect(response.data.user.postsCount).toBeTypeOf('number');
expect(response.data.user.verified).toBeTypeOf('boolean');
```

**`expect.any(Constructor)`** is an asymmetric matcher for type checking inside `toMatchObject` or `toEqual`:

```typescript
expect(response.data.user).toMatchObject({
  _id: expect.any(String),
  postsCount: expect.any(Number),
  verified: expect.any(Boolean),
});
```

Note: `expect.any(String)` uses the constructor (`String`), not the type name string (`'string'`). `toBeTypeOf('string')` uses the type name string. They are different matchers with different syntax.

#### Object Matchers

**`toHaveProperty(keyPath)`** and **`toHaveProperty(keyPath, value)`** check that a property exists (and optionally has a specific value):

```typescript
// Check existence
expect(response.data).toHaveProperty('user');
expect(response.data.user).toHaveProperty('_id');

// Check existence and value
expect(response.data).toHaveProperty('message', 'User login successfully');

// Check nested property with dot notation
expect(response.data).toHaveProperty('user.username', 'vitest_alice_001');

// Check nested property with array notation
expect(response.data).toHaveProperty(['user', 'email'], 'alice@example.com');
```

**`toMatchObject(object)`** is a partial match. The received object must contain all keys and values in the expected object, but may contain additional keys. This is the most frequently used object matcher in API testing:

```typescript
// The response may have more fields than listed — that's fine
expect(response.data.user).toMatchObject({
  username: 'vitest_alice_001',
  postsCount: 0,
});

// Combining with expect.any for dynamic values
expect(response.data.user).toMatchObject({
  _id: expect.any(String),
  username: 'vitest_alice_001',
  email: 'alice@example.com',
});
```

**`expect.objectContaining(object)`** is the asymmetric version of `toMatchObject`. Use it inside `toEqual`, `toMatchObject`, or `expect.arrayContaining` when you need partial matching in a nested position:

```typescript
expect(response.data).toEqual(
  expect.objectContaining({
    user: expect.objectContaining({
      username: 'vitest_alice_001',
    }),
  })
);
```

**The key difference** between `toMatchObject`, `toHaveProperty`, and `expect.objectContaining`:
- `toMatchObject`: top-level partial match of the `expect(value)` object
- `toHaveProperty`: checks for a single specific property
- `expect.objectContaining`: partial match in a nested position inside another matcher

#### Array Matchers

**`toHaveLength(n)`** checks the `.length` property:

```typescript
expect(response.data.posts).toHaveLength(3);
expect(response.data.posts).toHaveLength(0); // empty array
```

**`expect.arrayContaining([...])`** checks that the received array contains all elements in the expected array (order-independent, subset check):

```typescript
const posts = response.data.posts;
expect(posts).toEqual(
  expect.arrayContaining([
    expect.objectContaining({ _id: createdPostId }),
  ])
);
// passes if the array contains at least one post with this _id
// additional posts are fine
```

The powerful combination `toEqual(expect.arrayContaining([expect.objectContaining({...})]))` is one of the most useful array assertion patterns in API testing. It checks that a list contains at least one item matching a partial shape, without caring about the list's length, order, or other items.

#### Custom Assertions with toSatisfy

**`toSatisfy(fn)`** lets you write a custom assertion when no built-in matcher fits:

```typescript
// Check that a URL is a valid Cloudinary URL
expect(response.data.user.profilePicture).toSatisfy(
  (url: string) => url.startsWith('https://res.cloudinary.com/') && url.includes('/image/')
);

// Check JWT format (three segments)
expect(jwtString).toSatisfy(
  (s: string) => s.split('.').length === 3
);

// Check MongoDB ObjectId format
expect(response.data.user._id).toSatisfy(
  (id: string) => /^[0-9a-f]{24}$/.test(id)
);
```

The function passed to `toSatisfy` must return `true` for the assertion to pass. The error message shows the received value but not the expectation — so add a comment explaining what the function checks.

#### Negation with .not

Every matcher can be negated with `.not`:

```typescript
// Security assertions — most important use of .not
expect(response.data.user).not.toHaveProperty('password');
expect(response.data.user).not.toHaveProperty('passwordHash');
expect(response.data).not.toHaveProperty('internalId');

// Negative status code assertions
expect(response.status).not.toBe(500);

// Ensuring an optional field is absent when it should be
expect(response.data.user).not.toHaveProperty('twoFactorSecret');
```

`.not` assertions are particularly valuable in security testing. You cannot exhaustively test all fields that should be absent, but you can test the ones you know should never appear. Any time you add a new sensitive field to your data model, add a `.not.toHaveProperty` assertion to your tests.

### 5.3 Positive Assertions

A complete positive assertion checks all relevant dimensions of a successful response. For `POST /auth/signin` returning 200, here is what a thorough set of assertions looks like:

```typescript
describe('POST /auth/signin - success', () => {
  let response!: AxiosResponse;

  beforeAll(async () => {
    response = await axios.post(
      `${BASE_URL}/auth/signin`,
      { username: TEST_USERNAME, password: TEST_PASSWORD },
      { validateStatus: () => true }
    );
  });

  describe('1. Status code', () => {
    it('returns 200', () => {
      expect(response.status).toBe(200);
    });
  });

  describe('2. Exact values', () => {
    it('returns success message', () => {
      expect(response.data.message).toBe('User login successfully');
    });

    it('returns correct username', () => {
      expect(response.data.user.username).toBe(TEST_USERNAME);
    });
  });

  describe('3. Shape', () => {
    it('user has _id field that is a string', () => {
      expect(response.data.user._id).toBeTypeOf('string');
    });

    it('user has postsCount that is a non-negative number', () => {
      expect(response.data.user.postsCount).toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(0);
    });

    it('user has followersCount and followingCount', () => {
      expect(response.data.user).toMatchObject({
        followersCount: expect.any(Number),
        followingCount: expect.any(Number),
      });
    });
  });

  describe('4. Security', () => {
    it('does not return password field', () => {
      expect(response.data.user).not.toHaveProperty('password');
    });

    it('response has Content-Type application/json', () => {
      expect(response.headers['content-type']).toContain('application/json');
    });
  });
});
```

This covers five of the seven assertion dimensions: status code, exact values, shape, security properties, and headers. (Timing and state changes are more appropriate for dedicated performance and integration tests.)

### 5.4 Negative Assertions

Negative assertions — tests against error paths — are equally important as positive assertions. The sign-in endpoint should refuse invalid credentials, enforce validation, and never return user data for failed requests.

```typescript
describe('POST /auth/signin - invalid credentials', () => {
  let response!: AxiosResponse;

  beforeAll(async () => {
    response = await axios.post(
      `${BASE_URL}/auth/signin`,
      { username: TEST_USERNAME, password: 'wrong_password_that_will_fail' },
      { validateStatus: () => true }
    );
  });

  it('returns 401 for wrong password', () => {
    expect(response.status).toBe(401);
  });

  it('returns an error message', () => {
    expect(response.data.message).toBeDefined();
    expect(response.data.message).toBeTypeOf('string');
  });

  it('does not return user data', () => {
    expect(response.data).not.toHaveProperty('user');
  });

  // IMPORTANT: username enumeration resistance
  // The error message should NOT reveal whether the username exists
  it('error message is generic, not specific about which field was wrong', () => {
    const message = response.data.message as string;
    expect(message).not.toContain('username does not exist');
    expect(message).not.toContain('invalid username');
  });
});
```

The username enumeration test is a real security assertion. If an API returns different error messages for "username not found" versus "wrong password," an attacker can enumerate valid usernames by sending requests with different usernames and checking which produces which message. A well-designed API returns the same generic message for both cases.

### 5.5 Shape Validation with toMatchObject

`toMatchObject` is the workhorse of shape validation. It checks that a subset of fields have the right values or types, without requiring the full object to match exactly. This makes tests resilient to non-breaking API additions (new fields being added) while still catching field removals and type changes.

**Full match vs partial match**:

```typescript
// BRITTLE: full match breaks when API adds fields
expect(response.data.user).toEqual({
  _id: '6612a3b7e2c1d4f0a8b9e123',
  username: 'vitest_alice_001',
  email: 'alice@example.com',
  postsCount: 0,
  followersCount: 0,
  followingCount: 0,
});

// RESILIENT: partial match survives non-breaking additions
expect(response.data.user).toMatchObject({
  username: 'vitest_alice_001',
  email: 'alice@example.com',
  postsCount: expect.any(Number),
  followersCount: expect.any(Number),
  followingCount: expect.any(Number),
});
```

The partial match version will continue to pass when the API adds a `lastLoginAt` field or any other new field. It will fail if `username`, `email`, or the count fields are removed or change type.

**When to use exact values vs `expect.any(Type)`**:

Use exact values for:
- Values you created in the test setup (username, email you specified)
- Constant values that should never change (specific message strings)
- Values you explicitly set in a PATCH/PUT request (updated fields)

Use `expect.any(Type)` for:
- Generated IDs (`_id`, `authId`)
- Timestamps (`createdAt`, `updatedAt`)
- Computed counts that may change based on other tests
- URLs that contain generated content (Cloudinary URLs)

### 5.6 One Request, Many Checks

The central pattern of this chapter put into practice: one `beforeAll` request, exhaustive assertions across multiple `it` blocks.

Here is a complete, production-quality test file for `POST /auth/signup`:

```typescript
import axios, { AxiosResponse } from 'axios';
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';
import { config } from '../../src/config';
import { TEST_CLEANUP_SECRET } from '../../src/fixtures';

describe('POST /auth/signup', () => {
  const username = `vitest_${faker.internet.username().toLowerCase().replace(/[^a-z0-9]/g, '')}_${Date.now()}`;
  const email = `${username}@example.com`;
  const password = 'Test1@Password';
  let authId: string;
  let response!: AxiosResponse;

  beforeAll(async () => {
    response = await axios.post(
      `${BASE_URL}/auth/signup`,
      { username, email, password },
      { validateStatus: () => true }
    );
    authId = response.data?.user?.authId;
  });

  afterAll(async () => {
    if (authId) {
      await axios.delete(`${BASE_URL}/test/cleanup/user/${authId}`, {
        headers: { 'x-test-secret': TEST_CLEANUP_SECRET },
        validateStatus: () => true,
      });
    }
  });

  describe('1. Status code', () => {
    it('returns 201 Created', () => {
      expect(response.status).toBe(201);
    });
  });

  describe('2. Exact values', () => {
    it('returns success message', () => {
      expect(response.data.message).toBe('User created successfully');
    });

    it('user.username matches what was sent', () => {
      expect(response.data.user.username).toBe(username);
    });

    it('user.email matches what was sent', () => {
      expect(response.data.user.email).toBe(email);
    });
  });

  describe('3. Shape', () => {
    it('user._id is a 24-character hex string', () => {
      expect(response.data.user._id).toMatch(/^[0-9a-f]{24}$/);
    });

    it('user has zero postsCount on creation', () => {
      expect(response.data.user.postsCount).toBe(0);
    });

    it('user has zero followersCount on creation', () => {
      expect(response.data.user.followersCount).toBe(0);
    });

    it('user has zero followingCount on creation', () => {
      expect(response.data.user.followingCount).toBe(0);
    });

    it('user object has all expected fields', () => {
      expect(response.data.user).toMatchObject({
        _id: expect.any(String),
        username: expect.any(String),
        email: expect.any(String),
        postsCount: expect.any(Number),
        followersCount: expect.any(Number),
        followingCount: expect.any(Number),
      });
    });
  });

  describe('4. Security', () => {
    it('does not expose password in response', () => {
      expect(response.data.user).not.toHaveProperty('password');
    });

    it('does not expose password hash in response', () => {
      expect(response.data.user).not.toHaveProperty('passwordHash');
    });

    it('response Content-Type is application/json', () => {
      expect(response.headers['content-type']).toContain('application/json');
    });
  });
});
```

This test file demonstrates:
- Unique username generation using `faker` and a timestamp suffix (avoids conflicts with other tests)
- One request in `beforeAll`, many tests on the shared response
- Cleanup in `afterAll` using the test cleanup endpoint
- `validateStatus: () => true` on both the test request and the cleanup request
- Assertions across all five major dimensions for a create endpoint

**Key Points**

- Assert at the right level of specificity: exact values for stable, known data; type/shape assertions for dynamic data.
- `toBe` is for primitives (===). `toEqual` is for deep object/array comparison. `toMatchObject` is for partial matching. Learn the difference — using the wrong one causes subtle test failures.
- `.not` negation is essential for security assertions. Always test that sensitive fields (password, internal IDs) are absent from responses.
- `toMatchObject` with `expect.any(Type)` produces resilient shape assertions that survive non-breaking API additions.
- The `toEqual(expect.arrayContaining([expect.objectContaining({...})]))` pattern is the standard way to assert that an array contains at least one item matching a partial shape.
- `toSatisfy(fn)` is your escape hatch for custom assertions when no built-in matcher fits the situation.

**Exercises**

The following exercises use the Chatty API at `https://api.codeandtest.com/api/v1`. For each exercise, create a test file, make one request in `beforeAll`, and write the specified assertions. Run your tests with `npm test` after each exercise.

1. **Status code basics.** Call `GET /` (the API health check, if it exists) or `GET /users/nonexistent-user-xyz`. Use `validateStatus: () => true`. Write three assertions: (a) the status code is a number, (b) the status code is greater than or equal to 100, (c) the status code is less than 600. These assertions should pass for any valid HTTP response.

2. **String matchers.** Call `POST /auth/signin` with invalid credentials (wrong password). Assert: (a) `response.data.message` contains at least one character (is truthy), (b) `response.data.message` matches the regex `/^[A-Z]/` (starts with a capital letter), (c) `response.data.message` does NOT contain the word "stack" (error stack traces should not leak to clients), (d) `response.data.message` does NOT contain the word "mongo" (internal implementation details should not leak).

3. **Object shape matchers.** Call `POST /auth/signin` with valid credentials. Using `toMatchObject`, assert that `response.data.user` contains exactly these fields with these types: `_id` (any String), `username` (any String), `email` (any String), `postsCount` (any Number), `followersCount` (any Number), `followingCount` (any Number). Then add a `toHaveProperty` assertion for each of these same fields individually. Note that both approaches pass — they are testing the same thing in different ways.

4. **Array matchers.** If the Chatty API has a list endpoint (such as `GET /posts`), test it. Assert: (a) `response.data` (or `response.data.posts`) is an array, (b) each element contains at least a `_id` field of type string, using `expect.arrayContaining([expect.objectContaining({...})])`. If the list endpoint requires authentication, skip this exercise until Part III.

5. **Security assertions.** Call `POST /auth/signin` with valid credentials. Write five security-focused assertions using `.not`: (a) `response.data.user` does not have a `password` property, (b) `response.data.user` does not have a `passwordHash` property, (c) `response.data.user` does not have a `salt` property, (d) `response.data` does not have an `internalError` property, (e) `response.data` does not have a `stackTrace` property.

6. **Exact vs. partial matching.** Call `POST /auth/signup` with a unique new username and email. Write two versions of the same assertion about `response.data.user.username`: (a) using `toBe` with the exact username you sent, (b) using `toMatch` with a regex that checks the username starts with `vitest`. Verify both pass. Then change the regex in (b) to require the username to contain a digit — if your username generator does not include digits, this should fail. Fix the regex so it passes again. This exercise teaches the spectrum from exact to pattern matching.

7. **Custom assertions with toSatisfy.** Call `POST /auth/signin` with valid credentials. Assert that `response.data.user._id` satisfies a function that checks: (a) it is a string, (b) it has exactly 24 characters, (c) it only contains hexadecimal characters (0-9 and a-f). Write the `toSatisfy` callback to check all three conditions. This is a custom MongoDB ObjectId validator.

8. **Number range assertions.** Call `POST /auth/signin` with valid credentials. Assert: (a) `postsCount` is greater than or equal to 0, (b) `followersCount` is greater than or equal to 0, (c) `followingCount` is greater than or equal to 0. Then add timing assertions: capture `Date.now()` before and after the `beforeAll` request (record `startTime` before, `endTime` after). Assert that `(endTime - startTime)` is less than 5000 (5 seconds). This is a basic performance assertion.

9. **Negation patterns.** For the same sign-in response, write a test using `.not.toMatchObject` to assert that the response body does NOT match `{ error: expect.any(String) }`. This verifies there is no error field in the success response. Also assert the response does NOT have a `statusCode` property at the top level (some error formats include `statusCode` as a field; success responses should not).

10. **Comprehensive assertion suite.** Choose one endpoint from the Chatty API and write the most complete set of assertions you can, covering all seven dimensions from Section 1.3: status code, exact values, shape and types, computed relationships, headers, security (absent fields), and (conceptually) state changes. Aim for at least 12 passing assertions on a single response. This exercise is open-ended: any endpoint is valid, and the goal is thoroughness, not brevity.

Write these tests in your file before reading the next chapter:

1. Write a test that uses toMatchObject with expect.any(String) and expect.any(Number) to assert the full error response shape from POST /signin.
2. On the same response, use toBeTypeOf to assert statusCode is a number and message is a string.
3. Use toMatch(/regex/) to assert the message is a non-empty string (pattern: /\S+/).

#### Postman Exercises

Create a folder named "Chapter 5" inside your Postman collection. Work through these tasks:

1. Create a folder "Chapter 05 — Assertions". Add a successful POST /signin request. In Tests: assert status 200, message equals "User login successfully", token is a string, user is an object.
2. Add pm.test("Password not exposed", () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().user).to.not.have.property("password")).
3. Add pm.test("Token has JWT format", () => { const token = pm.response.json().token; pm.expect(token.split(".").length).to.equal(3); }).
4. Add pm.test("set-cookie header present", () => pm.expect(pm.response.headers.get("set-cookie")).to.include("session=")).

> **Note:** Use the shared beforeAll pattern — one request per test group, not one per assertion.
