---

## The Test File for This Chapter

> **Lecture 15 — Posts with Media (Image & Video Uploads)**
> Run: `npm test tests/lecture-15/lecture.test.ts`

```ts
// Lecture 15 — Posts with Media: Images & Videos
// Run: npm test tests/lecture-15/lecture.test.ts

import axios from 'axios';
import { config } from '../../src/config';
import { TEST_AVATAR_IMAGE } from '../../src/fixtures';

const signinUrl     = `${config.BASE_URL}/signin`;
const signoutUrl    = `${config.BASE_URL}/signout`;
const postUrl       = `${config.BASE_URL}/post`;
const imagePostUrl  = `${config.BASE_URL}/post/image/post`;
const getAllUrl      = `${config.BASE_URL}/post/all/1`;
const imagesPageUrl = `${config.BASE_URL}/post/images/1`;
const updateImgUrl  = (id: string) => `${config.BASE_URL}/post/image/${id}`;

const IMAGE_POST_CONTENT = `Vitest image post ${Date.now()}`;
const PLAIN_POST_CONTENT = `Vitest plain post ${Date.now()}`;

let sessionCookie = '';
let imagePostId = '';
let plainPostId = '';

beforeAll(async () => {
  const loginRes = await axios.post(signinUrl, {
    username: config.TEST_USERNAME, password: config.TEST_PASSWORD,
  }, { validateStatus: () => true });
  const raw = loginRes.headers['set-cookie'];
  sessionCookie = Array.isArray(raw) ? raw[0] : (raw ?? '');

  // Create a plain post
  await axios.post(postUrl, {
    post: PLAIN_POST_CONTENT, bgColor: '#fff', privacy: 'Public', feelings: '',
  }, { headers: { Cookie: sessionCookie }, validateStatus: () => true });

  // Create an image post
  await axios.post(imagePostUrl, {
    post: IMAGE_POST_CONTENT,
    image: TEST_AVATAR_IMAGE,
    bgColor: '#fff', privacy: 'Public', feelings: '', profilePicture: '',
  }, { headers: { Cookie: sessionCookie }, validateStatus: () => true });

  // Find both post IDs
  const getRes = await axios.get(getAllUrl, { headers: { Cookie: sessionCookie }, validateStatus: () => true });
  for (const p of (getRes.data.posts ?? []) as { post: string; _id: string; imgId: string }[]) {
    if (p.post === IMAGE_POST_CONTENT) imagePostId = p._id;
    if (p.post === PLAIN_POST_CONTENT) plainPostId = p._id;
  }
});

afterAll(async () => {
  for (const id of [imagePostId, plainPostId]) {
    if (id) await axios.delete(`${config.BASE_URL}/post/${id}`, {
      headers: { Cookie: sessionCookie }, validateStatus: () => true,
    });
  }
  await axios.post(signoutUrl, {}, { headers: { Cookie: sessionCookie }, validateStatus: () => true });
});

// ─── 1. Create image post ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────

describe('1. Create image post', () => {

  it('status is 201', async () => {
    const res = await axios.post(imagePostUrl, {
      post: `Vitest img check ${Date.now()}`,
      image: TEST_AVATAR_IMAGE,
      bgColor: '#fff', privacy: 'Public', feelings: '', profilePicture: '',
    }, { headers: { Cookie: sessionCookie }, validateStatus: () => true });
    expect(res.status).toBe(201);
    // Clean up extra post
    const all = await axios.get(getAllUrl, { headers: { Cookie: sessionCookie }, validateStatus: () => true });
    const extra = all.data.posts?.[0];
    if (extra?._id && extra?._id !== imagePostId) {
      await axios.delete(`${config.BASE_URL}/post/${extra._id}`, { headers: { Cookie: sessionCookie }, validateStatus: () => true });
    }
  });

  it('message is "Post created with image successfully"', async () => {
    const res = await axios.post(imagePostUrl, {
      post: `Vitest img msg ${Date.now()}`,
      image: TEST_AVATAR_IMAGE,
      bgColor: '#fff', privacy: 'Public', feelings: '', profilePicture: '',
    }, { headers: { Cookie: sessionCookie }, validateStatus: () => true });
    expect(res.data.message).toBe('Post created with image successfully');
    const all = await axios.get(getAllUrl, { headers: { Cookie: sessionCookie }, validateStatus: () => true });
    const extra = all.data.posts?.[0];
    if (extra?._id && extra._id !== imagePostId) {
      await axios.delete(`${config.BASE_URL}/post/${extra._id}`, { headers: { Cookie: sessionCookie }, validateStatus: () => true });
    }
  });

});

// ─── 2. Get posts with images ─────────────────────────────────────────────────

describe('2. GET /post/images/:page', () => {

  it('status is 200', async () => {
    const res = await axios.get(imagesPageUrl, {
      headers: { Cookie: sessionCookie }, validateStatus: () => true,
    });
    expect(res.status).toBe(200);
  });

  it('response has posts array', async () => {
    const res = await axios.get(imagesPageUrl, {
      headers: { Cookie: sessionCookie }, validateStatus: () => true,
    });
    expect(res.data).toHaveProperty('posts');
    expect(Array.isArray(res.data.posts)).toBe(true);
  });

  it('our image post appears in the list', async () => {
    const res = await axios.get(imagesPageUrl, {
      headers: { Cookie: sessionCookie }, validateStatus: () => true,
    });
    const found = res.data.posts?.find((p: { _id: string }) => p._id === imagePostId);
    expect(found).toBeDefined();
  });

  it('plain post does NOT appear in images list', async () => {
    const res = await axios.get(imagesPageUrl, {
      headers: { Cookie: sessionCookie }, validateStatus: () => true,
    });
    const plainInImages = res.data.posts?.find((p: { _id: string }) => p._id === plainPostId);
    expect(plainInImages).toBeUndefined();
  });

});

// ─── 3. Update post with image ────────────────────────────────────────────────

describe('3. Update post image', () => {

  it('PUT /post/image/:postId returns 200', async () => {
    const res = await axios.put(updateImgUrl(imagePostId), {
      post: 'Updated with new image',
      image: TEST_AVATAR_IMAGE,
      bgColor: '#f0f0f0', privacy: 'Public', feelings: '', profilePicture: '',
    }, { headers: { Cookie: sessionCookie }, validateStatus: () => true });
    expect(res.status).toBe(200);
    expect(res.data.message).toBe('Post with image updated successfully');
  });

});

// ─── 4. Validation errors ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────

describe('4. Validation errors', () => {

  it('POST /post/image/post without image returns 400', async () => {
    const res = await axios.post(imagePostUrl, {
      post: 'No image here',
      bgColor: '#fff', privacy: 'Public', feelings: '', profilePicture: '',
    }, { headers: { Cookie: sessionCookie }, validateStatus: () => true });
    expect(res.status).toBe(400);
  });

  it('POST /post/image/post with invalid image format returns 400', async () => {
    const res = await axios.post(imagePostUrl, {
      post: 'Bad image',
      image: 'not-a-valid-image',
      bgColor: '#fff', privacy: 'Public', feelings: '', profilePicture: '',
    }, { headers: { Cookie: sessionCookie }, validateStatus: () => true });
    expect(res.status).toBe(400);
    expect(res.data.message).toContain('Image must be');
  });

  it('POST /post/image/post without cookie returns 401', async () => {
    const res = await axios.post(imagePostUrl, {
      post: 'No auth',
      image: TEST_AVATAR_IMAGE,
    }, { validateStatus: () => true });
    expect(res.status).toBe(401);
  });

});

// ─── 5. Assertion variants ────────────────────────────────────────────────────
//
// Introduces three assertion styles not used elsewhere in the course:
//   toMatch(/regex/)  — test a string against a regular expression
//   toBeGreaterThan   — numeric lower-bound check
//   toSatisfy(fn)     — custom predicate function for flexible assertions

describe('5. Assertion variants', () => {

  it('toMatch — profile picture URL starts with http or https', async () => {
    // toMatch(/^https?:\/\//) confirms the URL uses a proper web scheme.
    // Regex is more precise than toContain('http') which would miss the colon.
    const res = await axios.get(imagesPageUrl, {
      headers: { Cookie: sessionCookie }, validateStatus: () => true,
    });
    const post = res.data.posts?.find((p: { imgVersion: string; imgId: string }) => p.imgId);
    if (post?.imgVersion) {
      const profilePictureUrl = `https://res.cloudinary.com/${post.imgId}/v${post.imgVersion}`;
      expect(profilePictureUrl).toMatch(/^https?:\/\//);
    }
  });

  it('toBeGreaterThan — image post list has at least one item', async () => {
    // toBeGreaterThan(0) is clearer than toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(1) for "non-empty" semantics.
    const res = await axios.get(imagesPageUrl, {
      headers: { Cookie: sessionCookie }, validateStatus: () => true,
    });
    expect(res.data.posts?.length ?? 0).toBeGreaterThan(0);
  });

  it('toSatisfy — image post has a non-empty imgId (custom predicate)', async () => {
    // toSatisfy lets you express multi-condition checks as a plain function,
    // keeping the test readable without chaining multiple expects.
    const res = await axios.get(imagesPageUrl, {
      headers: { Cookie: sessionCookie }, validateStatus: () => true,
    });
    const posts = res.data.posts ?? [];
    expect(posts).toSatisfy((arr: { imgId?: string }[]) =>
      arr.some(p => typeof p.imgId === 'string' && p.imgId.length > 0),
    );
  });

});
```

## Chapter 16: Continuous Integration with GitHub Actions

### What CI/CD Means for API Testing

Continuous Integration (CI) is the practice of running your test suite automatically every time code is pushed to a shared repository. Continuous Deployment (CD) extends this by automatically deploying code when tests pass.

For API testing specifically, CI means that every developer on your team, every pull request, and every merge to main is validated against the full test suite — not just against what the developer remembered to test locally. No one can accidentally merge code that breaks the signup flow or the authentication system, because the CI pipeline will catch it and report the failure before the merge is allowed.

Without CI, test suites decay. Tests that pass locally but fail in other environments go undetected. New features break existing ones. The test suite becomes a vanity metric — something that passes in ideal conditions but provides no real safety net.

With CI, the test suite is the safety net. It is always running, always reporting, and always blocking merges that introduce regressions.

---

### Complete Annotated Workflow YAML

GitHub Actions uses YAML files in `.github/workflows/` to define CI pipelines. Here is a complete, annotated workflow file for the Chatty API tests:

```yaml
# .github/workflows/tests.yml
#
# This file defines the CI pipeline for the Chatty API test suite.
# It runs automatically on pushes and pull requests, and can be
# triggered manually from the GitHub Actions tab.

# Name shown in the GitHub Actions UI
name: API Tests

# Defines WHEN this workflow runs
on:
  # Run on every push to any branch
  push:
    branches: ['**']

  # Run on every pull request targeting any branch
  pull_request:
    branches: ['**']

  # Allow manual execution from the GitHub Actions tab
  workflow_dispatch:
    # Optional inputs available when triggering manually
    inputs:
      test_suite:
        description: 'Which test suite to run (e.g., tests/lecture-05/)'
        required: false
        default: 'all'
        type: string

# Concurrency: cancel in-progress runs when a new push arrives
# This prevents queue buildup when developers push rapidly
concurrency:
  group: ${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

# Define the jobs that make up this workflow
jobs:
  test:
    # The type of runner (virtual machine) to use
    # ubuntu-latest is the most common choice for Node.js projects
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    # Matrix strategy: run tests against multiple Node.js versions
    # This catches issues where code works in Node 18 but not Node 20
    strategy:
      matrix:
        node-version: [18, 20]
      # If one matrix job fails, don't cancel the others
      fail-fast: false

    steps:
      # Step 1: Check out the repository code
      # actions/checkout@v4 is the standard way to get your code
      - name: Checkout repository
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      # Step 2: Set up the specified Node.js version
      # The matrix.node-version variable comes from the strategy.matrix section above
      - name: Set up Node.js ${{ matrix.node-version }}
        uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: ${{ matrix.node-version }}
          # Cache npm dependencies for faster subsequent runs
          cache: 'npm'

      # Step 3: Install dependencies
      # npm ci is preferred over npm install for CI:
      # - Uses the exact versions from package-lock.json
      # - Fails if package-lock.json is out of sync with package.json
      # - Faster than npm install
      - name: Install dependencies
        run: npm ci

      # Step 4: Run the test suite
      # Environment variables come from GitHub Secrets (defined in repository settings)
      - name: Run API tests
        run: |
          if [ "${{ github.event.inputs.test_suite }}" = "all" ] || [ -z "${{ github.event.inputs.test_suite }}" ]; then
            npm test
          else
            npm test -- ${{ github.event.inputs.test_suite }}
          fi
        env:
          # These secrets are configured in:
          # Repository Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions → New repository secret
          BASE_URL: ${{ secrets.BASE_URL }}
          TEST_USERNAME: ${{ secrets.TEST_USERNAME }}
          TEST_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.TEST_PASSWORD }}
          TEST_EMAIL: ${{ secrets.TEST_EMAIL }}
          TEST_SECRET: ${{ secrets.TEST_SECRET }}
          DATABASE_URL: ${{ secrets.DATABASE_URL }}

      # Step 5: Upload test results as an artifact
      # This preserves the results even if the tests failed
      # 'if: always()' ensures this step runs even when previous steps fail
      - name: Upload test results
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        if: always()
        with:
          name: test-results-node-${{ matrix.node-version }}
          path: |
            test-results/
            coverage/
          # Keep artifacts for 30 days
          retention-days: 30
```

---

### GitHub Secrets Setup

Secrets are encrypted environment variables stored in your GitHub repository settings. They are injected into workflow runs as environment variables, ensuring sensitive values like API credentials never appear in your repository's code or logs.

To add secrets to your repository:

1. Navigate to your repository on GitHub
2. Click **Settings** in the top navigation
3. In the left sidebar, click **Secrets and variables**, then **Actions**
4. Click **New repository secret**
5. Enter the name and value, then click **Add secret**

For the Chatty API test suite, you need these secrets:

| Secret Name | Description | Example Value |
|-------------|-------------|---------------|
| `BASE_URL` | The Chatty API base URL | `https://api.codeandtest.com/api/v1` |
| `TEST_USERNAME` | The pre-existing test user's username | `vitest_permanent_user` |
| `TEST_PASSWORD` | The test user's password | `TestPass123!` |
| `TEST_EMAIL` | The test user's email address | `testuser@example.com` |
| `TEST_SECRET` | The test cleanup endpoint secret | `your-test-secret-here` |
| `DATABASE_URL` | MongoDB Atlas connection string | `mongodb+srv://readonly:...` |

Secrets are masked in GitHub Actions logs. If a workflow step accidentally logs a secret's value, GitHub replaces it with `***`.

---

### Advanced: Path Filters and Conditional Execution

For large repositories, you may want tests to run only when relevant files change:

```yaml
# Only run API tests when tests/ or package.json change
on:
  push:
    paths:
      - 'tests/**'
      - 'package.json'
      - 'package-lock.json'
      - 'vitest.config.ts'
      - '.github/workflows/tests.yml'
  pull_request:
    paths:
      - 'tests/**'
      - 'package.json'
```

---

### Advanced: Multiple Job Dependencies

For more sophisticated pipelines where certain checks must pass before others run:

```yaml
jobs:
  lint:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: 20, cache: 'npm' }
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm run lint

  typecheck:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: 20, cache: 'npm' }
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm run typecheck

  test:
    # Only run tests after lint and typecheck pass
    needs: [lint, typecheck]
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    strategy:
      matrix:
        node-version: [18, 20]
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: ${{ matrix.node-version }}
          cache: 'npm'
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm test
        env:
          BASE_URL: ${{ secrets.BASE_URL }}
          TEST_USERNAME: ${{ secrets.TEST_USERNAME }}
          TEST_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.TEST_PASSWORD }}
          DATABASE_URL: ${{ secrets.DATABASE_URL }}
```

---

### Key Points

- CI runs your tests automatically on every push and pull request, catching regressions before they merge.
- Use `npm ci` instead of `npm install` in CI — it uses exact package-lock.json versions and fails if the lock file is inconsistent.
- The `strategy.matrix` with `node-version: [18, 20]` runs your tests against multiple Node.js versions simultaneously.
- `if: always()` on the artifact upload step ensures test results are preserved even when tests fail — this is essential for debugging CI failures.
- `concurrency: cancel-in-progress: true` prevents pipeline queues from building up when developers push rapidly.
- Never put secrets in YAML files. Use GitHub Secrets and reference them with `${{ secrets.SECRET_NAME }}`.

---

# .github/workflows/tests.yml

name: Chatty API Tests

on:
  push:
    branches: [main, develop]
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]
  workflow_dispatch:

jobs:
  test:
    name: Run Vitest (Node ${{ matrix.node-version }})
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    strategy:
      matrix:
        node-version: [18, 20]

    steps:
      - name: Checkout code
        uses: actions/checkout@v3

      - name: Setup Node.js ${{ matrix.node-version }}
        uses: actions/setup-node@v3
        with:
          node-version: ${{ matrix.node-version }}
          cache: 'npm'

      - name: Install dependencies
        run: npm ci

      - name: Run Vitest
        run: npm test
        env:
          BASE_URL: ${{ secrets.BASE_URL }}
          TEST_USERNAME: ${{ secrets.TEST_USERNAME }}
          TEST_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.TEST_PASSWORD }}
          DATABASE_URL: ${{ secrets.DATABASE_URL }}

      - name: Upload test results
        if: always()
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: test-results-node-${{ matrix.node-version }}
          path: test-results/
          retention-days: 7
```

> **WHY:** The `matrix.node-version` list `[18, 20]` makes GitHub Actions spin up two separate job runners in parallel — one per Node version. Both must pass before a pull request can merge. This catches regressions caused by Node API differences and documents which versions the project supports. `npm ci` is used instead of `npm install` because it installs the exact versions in `package-lock.json`, making builds reproducible.

**Exercise 2** — Add all 4 required secrets to your GitHub repository

Navigate to your repository on GitHub: **Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions → New repository secret**.

Add these four secrets:

| Secret name | Value |
|---|---|
| `BASE_URL` | `https://api.codeandtest.com/api/v1` |
| `TEST_USERNAME` | your existing test account username |
| `TEST_PASSWORD` | your existing test account password |
| `DATABASE_URL` | your MongoDB Atlas connection string |

> **WHY:** Secrets are encrypted at rest and never printed in workflow logs, even if you accidentally `echo` them. Storing them as repository secrets rather than hardcoding them in the YAML file prevents credentials from appearing in your git history. The workflow references them as `${{ secrets.NAME }}` — GitHub substitutes the values at runtime in the runner's environment.

---

**Exercise 3** — Push a commit and verify both jobs pass in the Actions tab

```bash
git add .github/workflows/tests.yml
git commit -m "ci: add Vitest workflow with Node 18/20 matrix"
git push
```

Then open your repository on GitHub and click the **Actions** tab. You should see a workflow run with two parallel jobs: `Run Vitest (Node 18)` and `Run Vitest (Node 20)`. Both must show a green checkmark.

> **WHY:** Verifying in the Actions UI confirms the workflow file syntax is valid and that all four secrets are correctly configured. A common failure at this step is a secret name typo — the runner receives an empty string, `npm test` fails because `BASE_URL` is missing, and the error in the logs says `Missing env var: BASE_URL`.

---

**Exercise 4** — Add a concurrency group that cancels in-progress runs on new push

Add this block to `tests.yml` at the top level (same indentation as `on:` and `jobs:`):

```yaml
concurrency:
  group: ${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true
```

> **WHY:** Without a concurrency group, pushing two commits in quick succession starts two separate workflow runs. Both consume GitHub Actions minutes and both hit the production API, doubling the rate-limit pressure. `cancel-in-progress: true` automatically cancels the older run when a newer one starts for the same branch. `github.ref` scopes cancellation per branch so a push to `main` never cancels a run in progress on `develop`.

---

**Exercise 5** — Add a status badge to your README.md

Add this line near the top of `README.md`, replacing `YOUR_USERNAME` and `YOUR_REPO` with your GitHub handle and repository name:

```markdown
![Chatty API Tests](https://github.com/YOUR_USERNAME/YOUR_REPO/actions/workflows/tests.yml/badge.svg)
```

> **WHY:** The badge fetches its SVG from GitHub's badge endpoint in real time. It shows green passing or red failing on the repository's front page, giving any visitor instant visibility into the current health of the test suite without opening the Actions tab.

# .github/workflows/tests.yml

## Chapter 17: Containerizing Tests with Docker

### The "Works on My Machine" Problem

Software developers encounter a specific failure mode so frequently that it has its own iconic phrase: "it works on my machine." The code, tests, or build process succeeds in one environment but fails in another. The developer sees passing tests locally. The CI server sees failures. The QA engineer sees a different error than the developer does. The production server behaves differently from staging.

The root cause is environmental inconsistency. Different machines have different Node.js versions, different npm package versions, different operating system configurations, different environment variables. The software depends on all of these conditions being correct, but they are never explicitly stated or enforced.

Docker solves this by bundling the application and all of its dependencies into a container — a self-contained unit that runs identically on any machine with Docker installed. The container image specifies exactly which Node.js version to use, which packages to install, and what environment to run in. There is no ambiguity, no "it depends on what's installed," no version drift.

For a test suite specifically, Docker provides the additional benefit of running tests in a clean, isolated environment with no pollution from previous test runs or from the host machine's state.

---

### Complete Dockerfile

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile
# Defines the container image for running Chatty API tests

# Base image: official Node.js 20 on Alpine Linux
# Alpine is a minimal Linux distribution (~5MB) that keeps the image small
# Use a specific version (20-alpine) rather than 'latest' for reproducibility
FROM node:20-alpine

# Set the working directory inside the container
# All subsequent commands run from this directory
# /app is conventional for Node.js applications
WORKDIR /app

# Copy ONLY the package files first (before the rest of the code)
# This is the critical Docker layer caching optimization:
# If package.json and package-lock.json haven't changed, Docker reuses
# the cached npm install layer from a previous build — saving minutes
COPY package*.json ./

# Install dependencies using the exact versions in package-lock.json
# --ci is the same as npm ci — deterministic, exact versions
RUN npm ci

# Copy the rest of the project files
# This happens AFTER npm ci so that code changes don't invalidate
# the npm install cache layer
COPY . .

# The command to run when a container starts from this image
# This is the DEFAULT command and can be overridden at docker run time
CMD ["npm", "test"]
```

The comment about layer caching deserves further explanation because it is one of the most important Dockerfile optimization patterns.

Docker builds images as a series of layers. Each instruction in a Dockerfile creates a layer. When you rebuild an image, Docker reuses cached layers from the previous build — up until the first layer that changed. If you `COPY . .` before `RUN npm ci`, then any change to any source file invalidates the cache for all subsequent layers, including the expensive `npm ci` step. By copying `package*.json` first and running `npm ci` before copying source code, you ensure that `npm ci` only reruns when your dependencies actually change — not on every code edit.

---

### RUN vs CMD: Build Time vs Runtime

The distinction between `RUN` and `CMD` is fundamental to understanding Dockerfiles.

`RUN` executes a command during the image build process and commits the result as a new layer. It is for tasks that should happen once when building the image: installing packages, compiling code, downloading assets.

`CMD` specifies the default command to execute when a container starts from the image. It does not run during the build. It runs every time someone does `docker run`. It can be overridden by arguments to `docker run`.

```dockerfile
# These run during BUILD (docker build .)
RUN npm ci
RUN npm run build

# This runs during RUNTIME (docker run ...)
CMD ["npm", "test"]
```

---

### The .dockerignore File

Just as `.gitignore` prevents files from being committed to git, `.dockerignore` prevents files from being included in the Docker build context. Without it, `COPY . .` would copy `node_modules/` (potentially gigabytes), `.env` files (credentials), and other irrelevant files into the image.

```
# .dockerignore

# Never copy the local node_modules — they're installed fresh by npm ci
node_modules/

# Never include environment files — secrets are injected at runtime
.env
.env.*
.env.local
.env.test.local

# Exclude coverage and test result output directories
coverage/
test-results/

# Exclude Docker-related files themselves (optional, for clarity)
Dockerfile
.dockerignore
docker-compose.yml

# Exclude editor metadata
.vscode/
.idea/
*.swp
*.swo

# Exclude git internals
.git/
.gitignore

# Exclude documentation build output
docs/build/
```

---

### Building and Running the Test Container

```bash
# Build the image, tagging it as 'chatty-tests'
docker build -t chatty-tests .

# Run all tests using an .env file for credentials
# --env-file reads KEY=VALUE pairs from the file and injects them as environment variables
docker run --env-file .env chatty-tests

# Run a specific test suite by overriding the CMD
# Everything after the image name replaces the CMD directive
docker run --env-file .env chatty-tests npm test tests/lecture-05/

# Run with individual environment variables (useful when .env file isn't available)
docker run \
  -e BASE_URL=https://api.codeandtest.com/api/v1 \
  -e TEST_USERNAME=myuser \
  -e TEST_PASSWORD=MyPass123! \
  chatty-tests

# Run interactively to debug a failing test
docker run -it --env-file .env --entrypoint sh chatty-tests
# Inside the container: npm test tests/lecture-12/ -- --reporter=verbose
```

---

### docker-compose.yml for Test Orchestration

For more complex scenarios — multiple service dependencies, specific network configurations, volume mounts for output artifacts — `docker-compose.yml` provides a declarative configuration:

```yaml
# docker-compose.yml
version: '3.8'

services:
  api-tests:
    # Build from the Dockerfile in the current directory
    build:
      context: .
      dockerfile: Dockerfile

    # Load environment variables from .env file
    # .env is excluded from .dockerignore — use your local .env file
    env_file:
      - .env

    # Mount volumes to retrieve test results from the container
    volumes:
      # Map the container's /app/test-results to ./test-results on the host
      # This allows you to read test reports after the container stops
      - ./test-results:/app/test-results
      - ./coverage:/app/coverage

    # Override the default CMD to run specific tests
    # Remove this line to run all tests
    # command: npm test tests/lecture-14/

    # Run tests once and exit (no restart)
    restart: 'no'
```

With this file, running all tests is:

```bash
docker-compose up --build
```

And the test results are available in `./test-results/` and `./coverage/` on the host machine after the container exits.

---

### Multi-Stage Build Pattern

For production deployments, a multi-stage build reduces the final image size by separating the build environment from the runtime environment. For test suites, this pattern is less critical, but it illustrates the principle:

```dockerfile
# Stage 1: Build / Dependency Installation
FROM node:20-alpine AS deps
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci

# Stage 2: Test Runner
FROM node:20-alpine AS test-runner
WORKDIR /app

# Copy only what's needed from the deps stage
COPY --from=deps /app/node_modules ./node_modules

# Copy source files
COPY . .

# Run tests
CMD ["npm", "test"]
```

---

### Docker in GitHub Actions

In GitHub Actions, Docker containers can be used to provide consistent environments. There are two approaches.

**Approach 1: Build and run the Docker image in the workflow**

```yaml
jobs:
  test-in-docker:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Build test image
        run: docker build -t chatty-tests .

      - name: Run tests in Docker
        run: |
          docker run \
            -e BASE_URL=${{ secrets.BASE_URL }} \
            -e TEST_USERNAME=${{ secrets.TEST_USERNAME }} \
            -e TEST_PASSWORD=${{ secrets.TEST_PASSWORD }} \
            -e DATABASE_URL=${{ secrets.DATABASE_URL }} \
            chatty-tests
```

**Approach 2: Use a container image for the job itself**

```yaml
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    container:
      image: node:20-alpine
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm test
        env:
          BASE_URL: ${{ secrets.BASE_URL }}
```

For most projects, Approach 1 provides the best combination of control and debuggability.

---

### Key Points

- Docker solves the "works on my machine" problem by packaging the test environment alongside the test code in a container image.
- Copy `package*.json` before source code, then run `npm ci` — this maximizes Docker layer cache reuse and keeps rebuilds fast.
- `RUN` executes during image build; `CMD` is the default runtime command and can be overridden with `docker run image npm test specific/suite`.
- `.dockerignore` must exclude `node_modules/` and `.env` files — the former for size, the latter for security.
- `docker run --env-file .env` is the standard way to pass credentials to a container without embedding them in the image.
- In GitHub Actions, use `-e KEY=${{ secrets.SECRET_NAME }}` to pass GitHub Secrets as environment variables to Docker run commands.

# Dockerfile

# Use the official Node 20 Alpine image
# Alpine is a minimal Linux distribution — the image is ~130 MB instead of ~900 MB
FROM node:20-alpine

# Set the working directory inside the container
WORKDIR /app

# Copy package files first so Docker can cache the npm install layer
# If only source files change, Docker reuses the cached node_modules layer
COPY package*.json ./

# Clean install matching package-lock.json exactly — same as CI
RUN npm ci

# Copy all source and test files into the container
COPY . .

# Default command: run the test suite
CMD ["npm", "test"]
```

> **WHY:** Copying `package*.json` before the rest of the source files is the most important Docker performance pattern. Because Docker caches each layer, if you only change a test file then `npm ci` (the slow step) is not re-run — Docker reuses the cached `node_modules` layer. `node:20-alpine` is used rather than `node:20` because the Alpine variant is roughly 7x smaller, reducing both pull time and the attack surface.

---

**Exercise 2** — Create a `.dockerignore` file

```
node_modules
.env
coverage
test-results
.git
*.log
```

> **WHY:** `.dockerignore` works like `.gitignore` but for the `docker build` context. Without it, `COPY . .` would copy `node_modules` (hundreds of megabytes) into the build context, massively slowing the build. More critically, `.env` must be excluded to prevent your local secrets from being baked into the image — the container receives secrets at runtime via `--env-file`, not at build time.

---

**Exercise 3** — Build the image

```bash
docker build -t chatty-tests .
```

> **WHY:** `-t chatty-tests` gives the image a human-readable tag so you can reference it by name instead of its SHA digest. The `.` at the end is the build context — the directory Docker reads `package*.json` and the rest of the source files from. Run this command whenever you add a new dependency or change `package.json`.

---

**Exercise 4** — Run tests inside the container

```bash
docker run --env-file .env chatty-tests
```

> **WHY:** `--env-file .env` reads each `KEY=VALUE` line from your local `.env` and passes them as environment variables into the container at runtime. This is the correct pattern — secrets never enter the image layer at build time. The test suite reads `BASE_URL`, `TEST_USERNAME`, `TEST_PASSWORD`, and `DATABASE_URL` from `process.env` as normal.

---

**Exercise 5** — Create `docker-compose.yml` with `env_file` and a volume mapping `test-results` to the host

```yaml
# docker-compose.yml
version: '3.8'

services:
  tests:
    build: .
    env_file: .env
    volumes:
      - ./test-results:/app/test-results
```

> **WHY:** The `env_file: .env` directive is the Compose equivalent of `docker run --env-file .env`. The `volumes` mapping mounts the host's `./test-results` directory into the container at `/app/test-results`. Any JUnit XML or coverage HTML written there by Vitest is immediately available on your host after the container exits — you can open the report in a browser without entering the container. Run with `docker compose up --build`.

## Chapter 18: Test Reporting and Coverage

### Why Reports Matter

The terminal output of `npm test` is ephemeral. It exists for the duration of the terminal session and then disappears. You cannot share it with a colleague who wasn't watching, attach it to a bug report, compare it to last week's run, or browse it after the CI pipeline completes.

Test reports persist your results. They transform the moment of test execution into a durable artifact that can be:

- Shared with product managers, business stakeholders, or clients
- Attached to pull requests as evidence of test coverage
- Stored in CI as build artifacts and compared across deployments
- Archived for compliance or audit purposes
- Used to identify trends over time (is test coverage increasing or decreasing?)

This chapter covers the three primary types of test output you should generate: Vitest reports for functional test results, coverage reports for line-by-line coverage analysis, and structured output formats (HTML, JUnit XML, JSON) for integration with CI tools and dashboards.

---

### Vitest Reporters

Vitest supports multiple built-in reporters, each suited to different contexts.

**Verbose reporter** — prints each individual test result to the terminal. Best for development and debugging.

**HTML reporter** — generates a browsable HTML file showing test results with filtering and search. Requires `@vitest/ui`.

**JUnit reporter** — generates XML in the JUnit format, the standard for CI systems. Jenkins, GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, and most other CI tools can consume JUnit XML to display test results in their UIs.

**JSON reporter** — generates a machine-readable JSON file useful for custom processing.

Configure reporters in `vitest.config.ts`:

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    // Run reporters in sequence
    reporters: [
      'verbose',          // Always show verbose terminal output
      'junit',            // Generate JUnit XML for CI
      'json',             // Generate JSON for custom tools
      ['html', {}],       // Generate HTML report (requires @vitest/ui)
    ],

    // Configure output file paths for non-terminal reporters
    outputFile: {
      junit: './test-results/junit.xml',
      json: './test-results/results.json',
      html: './test-results/index.html',
    },

    // Global test timeout (10 seconds for API tests)
    testTimeout: 10000,

    // Environment variables available in all tests
    env: {
      BASE_URL: process.env.BASE_URL ?? 'https://api.codeandtest.com/api/v1',
    },
  },
});
```

Install the required packages:

```bash
npm install --save-dev @vitest/ui
```

---

### Coverage Configuration with @vitest/coverage-v8

Code coverage measures which lines of your source code are executed during tests. For an API test suite that calls a running API (black-box testing), source coverage is less relevant than for unit testing. However, if you have test helpers, utilities, custom validators, or data transformation code, coverage analysis ensures those are tested too.

Install the coverage package:

```bash
npm install --save-dev @vitest/coverage-v8
```

Configure in `vitest.config.ts`:

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts (coverage section)
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    reporters: ['verbose', 'junit', 'html'],
    outputFile: {
      junit: './test-results/junit.xml',
      html: './test-results/index.html',
    },

    coverage: {
      // Use V8's built-in coverage (fastest, no instrumentation needed)
      provider: 'v8',

      // Report formats to generate
      reporter: [
        'text',    // Print summary table to terminal
        'html',    // Generate browsable HTML report
        'lcov',    // Generate LCOV format (consumed by CodeClimate, SonarQube, etc.)
        'json',    // Machine-readable JSON
      ],

      // Output directory for coverage reports
      reportsDirectory: './coverage',

      // Which files to include in coverage analysis
      // (your helper/utility files, not the test files themselves)
      include: ['src/**/*.ts'],

      // Which files to exclude
      exclude: [
        'src/**/*.test.ts',
        'src/**/*.spec.ts',
        'src/types/**',
        'src/**/*.d.ts',
      ],

      // Thresholds: fail the test run if coverage drops below these percentages
      // This is how you enforce coverage requirements in CI
      thresholds: {
        lines: 80,      // At least 80% of lines must be covered
        functions: 80,  // At least 80% of functions must be covered
        branches: 70,   // At least 70% of branches (if/else) must be covered
        statements: 80, // At least 80% of statements must be covered
      },

      // When true, fails the test run if thresholds are not met
      // (covered by the thresholds configuration above)
    },
  },
});
```

Run tests with coverage:

```bash
# Run all tests and generate coverage report
npm run coverage

# Add to package.json scripts:
# "coverage": "vitest run --coverage"
```

---

### Reading the HTML Coverage Report

After running coverage, open `./coverage/index.html` in a browser. You will see a table listing all covered files with four metrics:

- **Statements**: Individual executable statements (assignments, function calls, etc.)
- **Branches**: Decision points (if/else, ternary operators, switch cases)
- **Functions**: Function definitions
- **Lines**: Physical lines of code

Clicking into a file shows the source code with color coding:

- **Green**: Lines that were executed at least once during tests
- **Red**: Lines that were never executed — these are your coverage gaps
- **Yellow**: Lines that were executed, but not all branches were taken

The goal is not 100% coverage — that is often impossible or requires tests that verify implementation details rather than behavior. The goal is meaningful coverage: every important code path is exercised, every error handler is tested, every validation case is verified.

---

### Setting Thresholds and Failing CI

Coverage thresholds turn coverage analysis from a passive metric into an active gate. When you set `thresholds.lines: 80`, Vitest will exit with a non-zero exit code if coverage drops below 80%. GitHub Actions interprets a non-zero exit code as a failed step, which fails the CI run.

This creates a safety net against coverage regression: a developer cannot merge code that reduces test coverage below your minimum, because the CI pipeline will block the merge.

Choose thresholds that are achievable with your current coverage, then gradually raise them as you add tests. Starting at 100% threshold when your current coverage is 45% creates frustration, not quality. Starting at 50% and raising it by 5% each sprint creates a sustainable improvement culture.

---

### JUnit XML Structure

JUnit XML is the universal format for test results in CI systems. Understanding its structure helps you debug CI integration issues.

```xml
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<testsuites name="vitest tests" tests="42" failures="2" errors="0" time="8.532">
  <!-- Each describe() block becomes a <testsuite> -->
  <testsuite
    name="Chapter 05: Authentication"
    tests="8"
    failures="0"
    errors="0"
    time="2.145"
    timestamp="2024-01-15T10:30:00"
  >
    <!-- Each it() block becomes a <testcase> -->
    <testcase
      classname="tests/lecture-05/lecture.test.ts"
      name="signs in successfully with valid credentials"
      time="0.312"
    />
    <testcase
      classname="tests/lecture-05/lecture.test.ts"
      name="returns token with correct structure"
      time="0.287"
    />
  </testsuite>

  <testsuite name="Chapter 12: Error Testing" tests="15" failures="2" errors="0" time="3.891">
    <testcase
      classname="tests/lecture-12/lecture.test.ts"
      name="Category 3: Wrong Values returns 400 with Invalid credentials for wrong password"
      time="0.445"
    />
    <!-- Failed test includes a <failure> element -->
    <testcase
      classname="tests/lecture-12/lecture.test.ts"
      name="failed login does not return a token"
      time="0.312"
    >
      <failure message="expected 200 to equal 400" type="AssertionError">
        AssertionError: expected 200 to equal 400
          at tests/lecture-12/security-assertions.test.ts:42:5
      </failure>
    </testcase>
  </testsuite>
</testsuites>
```

The key attributes are:

- `tests`: Total number of test cases in this suite
- `failures`: Number of tests that failed assertions (the test ran but assertions were wrong)
- `errors`: Number of tests that threw unexpected errors (the test itself crashed)
- `time`: Execution time in seconds

CI systems parse this XML and display the results in their own UI, often with diff views showing which tests are newly failing compared to the previous run.

---

### Newman CLI for Postman Collection Execution

If your team also maintains Postman collections alongside Vitest tests — common during the transition period when some tests live in Postman and some in Vitest — Newman provides a way to run Postman collections from the command line and generate HTML reports.

```bash
# Install Newman and the HTML extra reporter
npm install --global newman newman-reporter-htmlextra
```

Run a Postman collection with full options:

```bash
newman run ./collections/chatty-api.postman_collection.json \
  --environment ./collections/chatty-env.postman_environment.json \
  --delay-request 500 \
  --reporters cli,htmlextra \
  --reporter-htmlextra-export ./test-results/newman-report.html \
  --reporter-htmlextra-title "Chatty API Test Report" \
  --reporter-htmlextra-darkTheme
```

Key flags explained:

- `--delay-request 500`: Wait 500ms between each request. Critical for APIs with rate limiting.
- `--reporters cli,htmlextra`: Output to both the terminal and the HTML reporter simultaneously.
- `--reporter-htmlextra-export`: Specifies the output file path for the HTML report.
- `--reporter-htmlextra-title`: Sets the title displayed at the top of the HTML report.
- `--reporter-htmlextra-darkTheme`: Generates a dark-themed report (purely cosmetic).

---

### GitHub Actions Integration for All Reports

The complete CI workflow that generates and uploads all report types:

```yaml
# .github/workflows/tests-with-reports.yml
name: API Tests with Reports

on:
  push:
    branches: ['**']
  pull_request:
    branches: ['**']

concurrency:
  group: ${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      - name: Checkout repository
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Set up Node.js 20
        uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 20
          cache: 'npm'

      - name: Install dependencies
        run: npm ci

      - name: Create output directories
        run: mkdir -p test-results coverage

      - name: Run tests with coverage
        run: npm run coverage
        env:
          BASE_URL: ${{ secrets.BASE_URL }}
          TEST_USERNAME: ${{ secrets.TEST_USERNAME }}
          TEST_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.TEST_PASSWORD }}
          DATABASE_URL: ${{ secrets.DATABASE_URL }}

      # Upload test results — runs even if tests failed (if: always())
      - name: Upload JUnit test results
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        if: always()
        with:
          name: junit-test-results
          path: test-results/junit.xml
          retention-days: 30

      # Upload HTML test report
      - name: Upload HTML test report
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        if: always()
        with:
          name: html-test-report
          path: test-results/index.html
          retention-days: 30

      # Upload coverage report
      - name: Upload coverage report
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        if: always()
        with:
          name: coverage-report
          path: coverage/
          retention-days: 30

      # Publish JUnit results to GitHub's native test report view
      # This shows test results directly in the pull request check details
      - name: Publish test results to GitHub
        uses: EnricoMi/publish-unit-test-result-action@v2
        if: always()
        with:
          files: test-results/junit.xml
          check_name: 'API Test Results'
          comment_mode: always
```

With this configuration, every CI run produces:

1. Visible test status in the GitHub Actions tab
2. Test result comments on pull requests (via `publish-unit-test-result-action`)
3. Downloadable artifacts: JUnit XML, HTML report, coverage report
4. Coverage failure if thresholds are not met (configured in `vitest.config.ts`)

---

### A Complete vitest.config.ts

Bringing everything together into one production-ready configuration file:

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    // Test file discovery
    include: ['tests/**/*.test.ts'],
    exclude: ['node_modules/**', 'dist/**'],

    // Global test timeout: 10 seconds for API tests
    // (network calls can be slow, especially in CI)
    testTimeout: 10000,

    // Hook timeout: 30 seconds for beforeAll/afterAll
    // (creating/cleaning up test data can take longer)
    hookTimeout: 30000,

    // Run tests sequentially within each file (important for stateful API tests)
    // Change to 'concurrent' only if your tests are truly independent
    sequence: {
      concurrent: false,
    },

    // Reporter configuration
    reporters: process.env.CI
      ? ['verbose', 'junit', 'json']   // In CI: generate all machine-readable formats
      : ['verbose'],                    // Locally: just show terminal output

    outputFile: {
      junit: './test-results/junit.xml',
      json: './test-results/results.json',
    },

    // Coverage configuration
    coverage: {
      provider: 'v8',
      reporter: ['text', 'html', 'lcov'],
      reportsDirectory: './coverage',
      include: ['src/**/*.ts'],
      exclude: ['src/**/*.test.ts', 'src/types/**'],
      thresholds: {
        lines: 80,
        functions: 80,
        branches: 70,
        statements: 80,
      },
    },

    // Environment variables available to all tests
    // These are merged with process.env
    env: {
      BASE_URL: process.env.BASE_URL ?? 'https://api.codeandtest.com/api/v1',
    },
  },
});
```

---

### Key Points

- Reports persist test results beyond the terminal session. Generate at minimum a JUnit XML (for CI) and an HTML report (for humans).
- Configure reporters in `vitest.config.ts`. Use `process.env.CI` to activate machine-readable reporters only in CI environments.
- `@vitest/coverage-v8` uses V8's native coverage instrumentation — no code transformation required.
- Coverage thresholds (`thresholds.lines: 80`) make coverage an active CI gate. A drop below the threshold fails the build.
- The `if: always()` directive on GitHub Actions artifact upload steps is essential — without it, you can't get reports from failed test runs.
- Newman CLI provides HTML reporting for Postman collections with `--reporters cli,htmlextra`.
- JUnit XML structure: `<testsuites>` → `<testsuite>` → `<testcase>` (with optional `<failure>` element for failing tests).

Updated `vitest.config.ts`:

```ts
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';
import { config as dotenvConfig } from 'dotenv';
import { resolve } from 'path';

dotenvConfig({ path: resolve(__dirname, '.env') });

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    globals: true,
    testTimeout: 15000,
    reporters: ['verbose'],
    fileParallelism: false,
    env: {
      BASE_URL: process.env.BASE_URL ?? '',
      TEST_USERNAME: process.env.TEST_USERNAME ?? '',
      TEST_PASSWORD: process.env.TEST_PASSWORD ?? '',
    },

    coverage: {
      provider: 'v8',
      reporter: ['text', 'html', 'lcov'],
      include: ['src/**/*.ts'],
      exclude: ['src/**/*.d.ts', 'node_modules/**'],
      thresholds: {
        lines: 80,
        branches: 70,
        functions: 80,
        statements: 80,
      },
    },
  },
});
```

> **WHY:** `provider: 'v8'` uses Node.js's built-in V8 coverage engine — no source transformation, lower overhead, and works natively with TypeScript. `include: ['src/**/*.ts']` restricts coverage measurement to the helper modules in `src/`; without this, Vitest may count the test files themselves, inflating numbers. The three reporters serve different consumers: `text` for the terminal summary, `html` for interactive browsing, `lcov` for external tools like Codecov or SonarQube.

```

> **WHY:** JUnit XML is the universal format for test result files. Jenkins, GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, and most reporting dashboards consume it. The `process.env.CI` guard means the JUnit reporter only activates in CI environments — local runs keep the clean `verbose` output without generating an XML file you did not ask for. The `test-results/` directory is the same one mounted as a Docker volume and uploaded as a GitHub Actions artifact.

---

**Exercise 3** — Export Postman collection and environment; run Newman with `htmlextra` reporter

```bash
# Install Newman and the htmlextra reporter globally (or use npx)
npm install -g newman newman-reporter-htmlextra

# Run the collection
newman run chatty-collection.json \
  --environment chatty-env.json \
  --reporters cli,htmlextra \
  --reporter-htmlextra-export test-results/newman-report.html
```

> **WHY:** Newman is the CLI runner for Postman collections. The `htmlextra` reporter generates a rich HTML report with request/response details, pass/fail badges, and response times — far more readable than the default CLI output when sharing results with non-engineers. Exporting the Postman environment as a separate file keeps the collection portable; the environment file holds the `BASE_URL` and auth tokens, similar to how `.env` works for Vitest.

---

**Exercise 4** — Add coverage thresholds at `lines: 80`; watch it fail when lowered

In `vitest.config.ts`, the `thresholds` block from Exercise 1 already sets `lines: 80`. To watch the failure, temporarily lower it below your actual coverage:

```ts
// Temporarily set this to trigger a failure — then restore to 80
thresholds: {
  lines: 95,   // set artificially high to see the error, then change back to 80
},
```

Run:

```bash
npm run test:coverage
```

Expected failure output:

```
ERROR  Coverage for lines (72.45%) does not meet the threshold (95%)
```

Restore to `lines: 80` after observing the failure.

> **WHY:** Thresholds cause `vitest run --coverage` to exit with a non-zero code when coverage drops below the minimum. In CI this fails the workflow step and blocks the pull request from merging. Observing the threshold failure message first — then restoring the correct value — helps you understand what the CI pipeline will print if coverage regresses in the future.

---

**Exercise 5** — Update GitHub Actions to upload both JUnit and coverage artifacts

Add these two steps to the end of the `test` job in `.github/workflows/tests.yml`:

```yaml
      - name: Upload JUnit test results
        if: always()
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: junit-results-node-${{ matrix.node-version }}
          path: test-results/junit.xml
          retention-days: 14

      - name: Upload coverage report
        if: always()
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: coverage-report-node-${{ matrix.node-version }}
          path: coverage/
          retention-days: 14
```

Complete updated `tests.yml` with concurrency, both reporters, and both artifact uploads:

```yaml
name: Chatty API Tests

on:
  push:
    branches: [main, develop]
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]
  workflow_dispatch:

concurrency:
  group: ${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

jobs:
  test:
    name: Run Vitest (Node ${{ matrix.node-version }})
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    strategy:
      matrix:
        node-version: [18, 20]

    steps:
      - name: Checkout code
        uses: actions/checkout@v3

      - name: Setup Node.js ${{ matrix.node-version }}
        uses: actions/setup-node@v3
        with:
          node-version: ${{ matrix.node-version }}
          cache: 'npm'

      - name: Install dependencies
        run: npm ci

      - name: Run Vitest with coverage
        run: npm run test:coverage
        env:
          CI: true
          BASE_URL: ${{ secrets.BASE_URL }}
          TEST_USERNAME: ${{ secrets.TEST_USERNAME }}
          TEST_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.TEST_PASSWORD }}
          DATABASE_URL: ${{ secrets.DATABASE_URL }}

      - name: Upload JUnit test results
        if: always()
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: junit-results-node-${{ matrix.node-version }}
          path: test-results/junit.xml
          retention-days: 14

      - name: Upload coverage report
        if: always()
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: coverage-report-node-${{ matrix.node-version }}
          path: coverage/
          retention-days: 14
```

> **WHY:** `if: always()` is critical — it ensures the artifact upload step runs even when the test step fails. Without it, a test failure would skip the upload and you would have no evidence to debug from. The `${{ matrix.node-version }}` suffix in the artifact name prevents the two matrix jobs from overwriting each other's artifacts. `retention-days: 14` keeps artifacts long enough to review after a flaky run without accumulating them indefinitely.

> **Note:** No test files for this chapter — the deliverables are config changes and report files.

---

## The Config Files for This Chapter

> **Lecture 13 — Test Reporting: Vitest, Newman & Coverage**
> The updated `vitest.config.ts` with reporters and coverage configuration.

```ts
// vitest.config.ts — with full reporters and coverage
// Copy this to your project root to replace the basic vitest.config.ts

import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';
import { config as dotenvConfig } from 'dotenv';
import { resolve } from 'path';

dotenvConfig({ path: resolve(__dirname, '.env') });

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    globals: true,
    testTimeout: 15000,
    fileParallelism: false,

    // Reporters: verbose in local, JUnit in CI
    reporters: process.env.CI ? ['junit', 'verbose'] : ['verbose'],
    outputFile: {
      junit: 'test-results/junit.xml',
    },

    // Coverage — run with: npm run test:coverage
    coverage: {
      provider: 'v8',
      reporter: ['text', 'html', 'lcov'],
      include: ['src/**/*.ts'],
      thresholds: {
        lines: 80,
        functions: 80,
        branches: 70,
      },
    },

    env: {
      BASE_URL:      process.env.BASE_URL      ?? '',
      TEST_USERNAME: process.env.TEST_USERNAME ?? '',
      TEST_PASSWORD: process.env.TEST_PASSWORD ?? '',
      DATABASE_URL:  process.env.DATABASE_URL  ?? '',
    },
  },
});
```
